pituitary adenomas , monoclonal in origin , are the most common intracranial neoplasms .

####  Clinical Manifestations

Prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas are often asymptomatic. Prolactinomas can be manifested by hypogonadism and infertility, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and headache. Clinical manifestations associated with functioning pituitary adenomas include loss of height, weight, and bone density. Neurological and endocrine abnormalities are less common with most of the pituitary adenomas. The prolactinomas secrete prolactin, but the other pituitary adenomas that cause dysfunction are secreting either oxytocin, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH ), renin, gonadotrophins, antidiuretic hormone, growth hormone, and other hormones. Other associated symptoms include hypoglycemia, hypotension and polyuria.

####  Diagnosis

Diagnosis is made with the use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which is the best imaging modality for pituitary tumors. Virtually all nuclear power plants generate electricity by heating water to provide steam that drives a turbine connected to an electrical generator. Nuclear-powered ships and submarines either use a steam turbine directly for main propulsion, with generators providing auxiliary power, or else employ turbo-electric transmission, where the steam drives a turbo generator set with propulsion provided by electric motors. A limited number of steam turbine railroad locomotives were manufactured.

The steam turbine was originally invented in the mid 19th century to power ship propulsion, and in the early 20th century, its potential was recognized in other areas such as generating electricity, but the steam turbine in its existing form was not suitable for these other applications.

Development of the gas turbine, both for power generation and propulsion, led to the possibility of using the gas turbine to drive a steam turbine.

First experimental tests of such a system, the first in the UK was in 1958. The first commercial power plant to use a steam-turbine integrated gas turbine system was the R.J.S.S. Isambard Kingdom Brunel at Didcot in 1965.

Steam turbine 

A steam turbine is a type of steam turbine where the working fluid is water (or another steam-like fluid). The working gas is usually steam, but also air injected into the inlet of a boiler or a combustion chamber can drive it. In the case of nuclear power plants, it is the heating water for the reactor core. This is typically delivered to the turbine in the form of superheated steam, which allows more of the available energy to be converted, as steam is a low-temperature working fluid.

Components 
 The impeller typically uses an impeller wheel to accelerate the working fluid, which is generally a mixture of steam and air.
 In low speed turbines, the rotor surrounds the impeller, but in larger units the impeller is integrated into the turbine disc.

At the begin of the Holocene (~11,700 years ago), the Rhine occupied its Late-Glacial valley. As a meandering river, it reworked its ice-age braidplain. During the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), ice sheets spread widely over northern and central Europe and left an imprint on the topography of the Rhine foreland. There are now two important questions that the current research needs to address.

First, which ice sheet was responsible for this surface lowering? Differential uplift histories can help with identifying the relevant ice sheet and its corresponding contribution to the topography of the Rhine foreland. Second, how do geomorphic features on the river channel relate to these former ice sheet morphologies? In this study, we examine the Holocene sedimentary record of the river channel in the Rhine foreland in northern Germany. The presence of diked tributaries in the Holocene record suggests a high degree of ice-age related deformation is preserved in the topography of the region. However, no clear relationship is found between surface changes, ice, and diked tributaries. Extension causes the rock units as a whole to become longer and thinner. This is primarily accomplished through normal faulting and through the ductile stretching and thinning. Normal faults drop rock units that are higher below those that are lower. This is generally referred to as the "strike-slip system". The normal faulting may be on a single dipping plane, or may be on planes inclined and tilted with respect to each other.

For example, a large normal fault in western New Jersey, the Newark Valley Extensional Zone (see the red/light green line in the image below), is believed to have opened 5–6 million years earlier than many other extensional zones in the Mid-Atlantic region. A detailed mapping of the Newark Valley Zone has revealed that these are normal fault zones, with similar dipping structures on adjacent terrains, where the extensional zone appears as a thick green line with many overlapping features. A detailed mapping and study of the Newark Valley Normal Faults revealed a more complex picture than had been believed. The normal fault structures were found to contain numerous structures with depths and extents that are smaller than the expected normal faulting. These smaller units are known as seismographs and extensional overprints.

Tensional overprints are zones where the rock units are much thicker (up to an order of magnitude). Tensional overprints occur both on adjacent terrains as well in the Newark Valley Normal Faults. These smaller zones can be detected in maps of the Newark Valley Zone as the extensional overprints in the green areas (see below), but are also numerous in smaller zones on the adjacent terrains (red area).

Killer T cells are a sub-group of T cells that kill cells that are infected with viruses (and other pathogens), or are otherwise damaged or dysfunctional. As with B cells, each type of T cell recognizes a different antigen. Killer T cells are activated when their T cell receptor (TCR) binds to this specific antigen in a complex with the MHC Class I receptor of another cell. Activating a killer T cell marks the targeted cell for apoptosis.

Killer T cells play an important role in protecting the body from many common infectious pathogens. While not every individual will develop killer T cells, there are many factors that influence the number of killer T cells in a person’s system.

Our killer T cells can recognize several different types of infectious diseases, including many types of cancer.

Modern primality tests for general numbers n can be divided into two main classes, probabilistic (or "Monte Carlo") and deterministic algorithms. Deterministic algorithms provide a way to tell for sure whether a given number is prime or not. For example, trial division is a deterministic algorithm because, if performed correctly, it will always identify a prime number as prime and a composite number as composite. Unfortunately, trial division is usually an extremely slow and cumbersome method, so most of the prime number computations are handled using probabilistic primality tests.

Deterministic primality tests include the widely known Miller-Rabin test and the AKS primality test, which are generally preferred because of speed and efficiency. However, probabilistic primality tests are a better choice for general computing where speed is more important than the ability to test every single number in sequence. This is because a lot of numbers (composite numbers, for example), will be tested even if they're not primes; this is typically considered acceptable because the testing is relatively fast and efficient in a probabilistic sense.

The ability of the immune system to respond to pathogens is diminished in both the young and the elderly, with immune responses beginning to decline at around 50 years of age due to immunosenescence. Primary immunodeficiencies (PIDs) are defined as inherited disorders in which the adaptive and innate immune systems are reduced, compared to healthy subjects. The phenotypes are diverse, but one class of PID is the X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (XLA), which is found in male patients with X-linked recessive inheritance, including all patients with the congenital form of XLA due to *CD46* X-linked gene mutation, and one-half of XLA patients with later onset due to *DGKB* mutation. Treatment is based on replacement immune globulins in the early stage of the disease. During the 1970s-1990s, XLA patients also received immunoglobulin infusions but, due to potential morbidity and mortality secondary to immune complexes, these treatments were stopped. Uptake of O 2 from the air is the essential purpose of respiration, so oxygen supplementation is used in medicine. Treatment not only increases oxygen levels in the patient's blood, but has the secondary effect of decreasing resistance to blood flow in many types of diseased lungs, easing work load on the heart. Oxygen therapy is used to treat emphysema, pneumonia, some heart disorders (congestive heart failure), some disorders that cause increased pulmonary artery pressure, and any disease that impairs the body's ability to take up and use gaseous oxygen.

The most commonly employed procedure for delivering supplemental O 2 is the nose mask, which is designed to fit into the nostrils and supply a flow equal to ambient air O 2. These devices deliver a continuous flow that is proportional to the supply of air. Continuous O 2 flow is usually maintained for varying lengths of time.

More sophisticated delivery systems provide continuous and controlled continuous O 2 flow. Most of these employ an O 2 concentration sensor such as an O2-electrode, an O2-thermistor, or another device which senses O 2 content. The sensor generates a signal that controls the continuous O 2 flow. Flow can be set from a few mL/min up to 10L/min. Delivery is controlled by a controller that reacts to the output of the sensor by adjusting the amount of O 2 flowing to the patient. This may be an on-off demand system (in which the O 2 flow is controlled by an on-off system that turns the flow on and off at preset times), an on-demand system (in which the flow is controlled on demand when the sensor signal needs adjustment), or a "smart-pulse" system (in which the O 2 flow is controlled by a controller that "pumps up" as the sensor output decreases). In these systems O 2 flow is either continuous or occurs in short "pulses." The O 2 delivery may be timed to the patient's exercise or it may "smooth out" the patient's breathing rate

The purpose of this article is to report on a case of actinomycosis with clinical findings similar to periodontitis. Case report A 46-year-old female presented with recurrent throbbing pain on the right first and second molar of the mandible. Three weeks prior to this presentation the root planing had been performed in the above mentioned teeth. On examination the patient had erythematous - sore lesions on molars 1 and 2, as well as on the adjacent mucosa, extending from the crown of molar 1 to the crown of the second molar and the palate. Probing revealed a purulent discharge. Radiographically there was no radiographic evidence of periodontal disease. The biopsy was performed with a tooth brush for access and to avoid contamination of the surrounding healthy tissue. Histopathologically, the findings included the presence of granulomatous inflammations, abscesses, and sulfur granules around the tooth. There were no multinucleated giant cells. The patient was given erythromycin lactobionate and miconazole nitrate. The lesions gradually resolved, and the patient was lost to follow-up.

In some rural areas in the United Kingdom, there are dispensing physicians who are allowed to both prescribe and dispense prescription-only medicines to their patients from within their practices. The law requires that the GP practice be located in a designated rural area and that there is also a specified, minimum distance (currently 1.6 kilometres) between a patient's home and the nearest retail pharmacy. The Royal Pharmaceutical Society, which campaigns on behalf of the pharmacist and prescriber, argues that the dispensing of prescription medicines in a rural setting creates a significant and positive effect on the practice of general practice and that this is a valuable and essential service.

Australia 
As in New South Wales and Victoria, Australia, the dispensing of prescription-only medicine is provided by a Registered Hospital Pharmacist, a health profession which also practises physiotherapy, radiology and ultrasound.

The legislation providing for the dispensing of prescription medicines in Australia is outlined in the Therapeutic Goods, Prescribing and Poisons Act 1988 section 30 that enables pharmacists to act as dispensers in specific prescription-only medicines if required. Currently there are five medicines in this category: Atropisert, Asycamep, Clopamide, Domperidone and Propionic acid.

The first person to practise what appears to be the earliest modern retail pharmacy in Australia was George Huddell, a stonemason at Port Fairy, Victoria in 1840. However, he was not registered as a pharmacist. The first registered pharmacist to practise his profession was Thomas C. Campbell, who had practised as a physician in Western Australia before settling in Sydney in 1842 where he continued to trade as a druggist in George Street, Sydney. Both before and after the 1708 passage of the Foreign Protestants Naturalization Act, an estimated 50,000 Protestant Walloons and Huguenots fled to England, with many moving on to Ireland and elsewhere. In relative terms, this was one of the largest waves of immigration ever of a single ethnic community to Britain. Andrew Lortie (born André Lortie), a leading Huguenot theologian and writer who led the exiled community in London, became known for articulating their criticism of the Pope and the doctrine of transubstantiation during Mass.

Some, such as David Lort, a son of a Huguenot convert to Catholicism, came as refugees and settled in South Wales, where they established themselves in mining and agriculture. Others settled across Britain, such as in Nottingham and Bristol, while more returned to the towns and cities of Flanders and to France itself.

Contents

The French historian Marc Bloch, after having noted the fact that there can be no comprehensive history of the French Huguenots, nonetheless comments that, in that the period 1600-1730, in France, it was "the most violent outburst of persecution".[1] The Protestants were considered the most dangerous group to French society and in 1685, Cardinal Mazarin prohibited their gatherings. The persecution of Huguenots in France, however, was only the beginning of a much wider persecution of Protestants which would spread throughout Europe following the religious wars of the 16th and 17th centuries.

The first Huguenot community in Britain was established in 1570, but many British Protestants of French descent were already settled there in the late 15thcentury, having been forcibly transported to Scotland to build fortresses under James IV of Scotland from 1486 to 1492. By the early 17th century, there were a few dozen Scottish Huguenot families settled in Scotland.[2]

In Japan, at the end of the Asuka period (538–710) and the early Nara period (710–794), the men who fulfilled roles similar to those of modern pharmacists were highly respected. The place of pharmacists in society was expressly defined in the Taihō Code (701) and re-stated in the Yōrō Code (718). Ranked positions in the pre-Heian Imperial court were established; and this organizational structure remained largely intact until the Meiji Restoration (1868).

Around 1005, Gennō no Miya no Sukune no Hirō, was one of the last of the Nara Period pharmacists, and was the earliest member of the Nara Period pharmacists who has been excavated to date. He was believed to have come from Kyō-ku, Tokyo which has been dated back to the early 9th century.

He was an assistant to the imperial medicine man Gennō, who was in charge of the Imperial Court and was designated as the Imperial Medical Examiner, and he had responsibility for the selection of medicines to be prescribed and medicines to be dispensed to the emperor.

His grave has been excavated at Nikkō National Park and is dated back to 1005–1006. It is believed that he was also a professional poet, writer, and calligrapher. His remains are believed to be the earliest to have been excavated from the capital of Nara.
The contents in his grave were believed to come from different places, such as the Kōdaiji compound in Nara, as well as Tokyo, Ōmu and Kawaramachi.

Radiographic abnormalities (such as stem prominence), biomechanical abnormalities (such as varus malalignment), soft tissue abnormalities (such as leg length discrepancy, dislocation, subluxation, and muscle imbalance), systemic disorders (such as hyperparathyroidism), and infections (such as superficial or deep) may lead to periarticular pathological changes in the adjacent joints (Fig. 16.1) [ 1 ]. SOMETIMES things are not what they seem. Beneath the surfaces of Walter Hill's noisy biker musical Streets of Fire and John Boorman's urban thriller Point Blank are themes derived from the Arthurian cycle and the Grail romances. Ron Howard's Willow and George Miller's Mad Max series both draw on the kitty of motifs provided by The Hero with a Thousand Faces, a scholarly work of comparative mythology by the late Joseph Campbell.

I first heard of Joseph Campbell through Stanley Kubrick's Spartacus and his epic movie-within-a-movie treatment of the story of Lucius Apuleius. Now there's a book Campbell has inspired, his Hero with a Thousand Faces, which tells how the world is shaped by the stories which, over time, people have adapted to mean many things to many people.

The book, published in 1964, is the work of a prolific and ingenious American thinker. In it Campbell explains the origin, function and future of myth. He outlines his beliefs about the way stories are created, and the way human beings respond to storytelling. He has a wide and fascinating knowledge of mythology, and his ideas in this book give an idea of just how wide and detailed that knowledge must be to have been assembled from so many varied sources.

Campbell's aim in this book is to demonstrate how similar patterns, motifs and motif functions exist in myths from all over the world, and how every individual lives and learns by absorbing stories which embody these patterns. Campbell was, and is, a teacher, and he was also one of the leading authorities on mythology. His knowledge of the subject and his desire to communicate this knowledge to the public led him to make his ideas his life's work.

Land-based steam engines could exhaust much of their steam, as feed water was usually readily available. Prior to and during World War I, the expansion engine dominated marine applications where high vessel speed was not essential. It was however superseded by the British invention steam turbine where speed was required, for instance in warships, such as the dreadnought battleships, and ocean liners. A related innovation, the direct-drive steam engine was used on the land-based railways that became common in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

After World War I, many land-based steam engines, especially in the USA, were superseded by internal combustion or electric motors, which had the advantage of being infinitely adjustable for duty cycle control, and which had much better efficiency at high speeds, and thus became an important replacement for steam. By the 1930s diesel and electrical locomotives had overtaken steam traction.  Steam locomotive production ceased in the Western world after WWII, where diesel locomotives and electric propulsion have remained dominant. The steam ship was also phased out with the development of the diesel internal combustion engine.

Advantages and limitations
Steam locomotives can produce much higher power outputs than electric locomotives for a given number of horsepower, and have longer travel ranges. They can deliver these outputs even where no diesel or electric motor can be supplied without excessive cost and weight-loading. A small but significant amount of freight or passenger service is now being provided by steam locomotives in some locations, such as the tourist Pullman trains in the western USA, or the Royal Golden Eagle Trains operating by and under contract to the Canadian National Railway in the Canadian Rockies, or on the  narrow-gauge railways in parts of the British Columbia Coast.

Oxygen storage methods include high pressure oxygen tanks, cryogenics and chemical compounds. For reasons of economy, oxygen is often transported in bulk as a liquid in specially insulated tankers, since one liter of liquefied oxygen is equivalent to 840 liters of gaseous oxygen at atmospheric pressure and 20 °C (68 °F). Such tankers are used to refill bulk liquid oxygen storage containers, which stand outside hospitals and other institutions with a need for large volumes of pure oxygen gas. Liquefied oxygen is used in most industrial applications, with oxygen tanks being filled at the plant or job site. Liquefied oxygen is also used by many fire-fighting services (especially when water-based foam attacks the oxygen supply from a cylinder which contains an oxygen-based defoamer), as in water intoxication the rapid infusion of large volumes of fluid can cause a significant drop in blood gases that can be fatal within just a few minutes.

Liquefied carbon dioxide is transported in specially insulated CO2 transport tanks.

Many liquid hydrogen tankers are equipped with a cooling element (liquid nitrogen, solid cryogen, or heat sink) that extends from the bottom of the tank to a point above the liquid hydrogen. This is to prevent heat from being transferred into the liquid hydrogen due to pressure differences: a lower, colder temperature within a closed container creates a lower ambient temperature overall. Liquid hydrogen tankers are often also equipped with a cryogen ejector, which reduces the amount of storage space, but allows the fuel-free storage of a much larger tank.

Liquid oxygen is also used for underwater breathing and diving equipment, but due to its high freezing point (77 K, 2.19 K), a significant amount of power is required to liquefy it. The ability to make probabilistic decisions often helps algorithms solve problems more efficiently.

The first proof that it is useful to think of programs as random objects was given by Solomon Feferman in 1960. This proof, however, was a bit technical, and some readers thought of it as a mathematical curiosity and skipped reading it. Trioxygen (O 3) is usually known as ozone and is a very reactive allotrope of oxygen that is damaging to lung tissue. Ozone is produced in the upper atmosphere when O 2 combines with atomic oxygen made by the splitting of O 2 by ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Since ozone absorbs strongly in the UV region of the spectrum, the ozone layer of the upper atmosphere functions as a protective radiation shield for the planet. Although the lower levels of the atmosphere contain more O 2, oxygen is actually not as reactive as other elements.

A variety of materials that interact with O 2 and are used to produce ozone including the dyes in the plastic film used to make shopping bags. This interaction causes ozone to form on the plastic and be released in the shopping bags when they are opened. When used to treat wastewater, ozone tends to form a thin film on the surface of the water. When sunlight is shining on the film, more O 2 is absorbed into the material making it more reactive than it would be in any other condition. However, most of the sun's radiation (UV light) is in long wavelengths and ozone cannot be formed above the atmosphere under most natural conditions.

Ozone is a very strong oxidizing agent that can react with many other molecules, most commonly the components of organic matter, but it can damage any organic compound that it reacts with. Once ozone reacts with any molecule it usually breaks it up by forming a bond to oxygen atoms on the molecule and removing electrons from atoms on the molecule. Since ozone is a strong oxidizing agent, oxygen molecules in the atmosphere are almost always in an ionic form. Since ozone is unstable it is not released into the atmosphere in a free state.

Most influential among these was the definition of Turing machines by Alan Turing in 1936, which turned out to be a very robust and flexible simplification of a computer. But what Turing machines had to do (and did) is much broader than computers per se: for example, they can be seen as the canonical model of automata and formal languages, among other things. More recently, this work took some interesting forms and led to the development of various notations and concepts. Each sitting day, normally at 5 pm, MSPs decide on all the motions and amendments that have been moved that day. This "Decision Time" is heralded by the sounding of the division bell, which is heard throughout the Parliamentary campus and alerts MSPs who are not in the chamber to return and vote. At Decision Time, the Presiding Officer puts questions on the motions and amendments by reading out the name of the motion or amendment as well as the proposer and asking "Are we all agreed? Mr Speaker, is that agreed?" The presiding officer has no formal role in the MSPs' decisions, although he can make statements on motions within the debating period (and even the whole session) without objection.

The MSPs who do not return from their break return to the parliamentary campus to hear the motions and amendments they have decided to move and propose. The MSP who was in the chamber when the division bell rang is entitled to take the Speaker's chair to lead the debate on the motions and amendments that have been decided.

After the debates, the MSPs vote on the amendments. An amendment that is voted down cannot be added in amendments to the main motion.

The next day is the same, except that the MSPs consider the amendments to the amendments (second reading) rather than the amendments to the motion.

A key feature of the MSP process is that once a motion is lost, no subsequent motion can be put to the house. This "no-go' provision provides an opportunity at this stage for the MSP to change their minds on any contentious motions.
A motion may be lost on a "motion of no confidence in the speaker", a motion of "no confidence in the speaker's conduct", a motion of "no confidence in the speaker's conduct by more than 50 per cent of the membership of the assembly". When lost, motions of this type may be re-moved.

When Normans arrived in their lands, they found laws that originated in the pre-Norman period in Great Britain (Anglo-Saxon and Celtic). This form of political Islam, sometimes called radical Islam, has been responsible for Islamist upsurges in the Muslim world, most notable among them in Iran in 1979, in Afghanistan in the 1980s, and in Algeria in the 1990s, after it first began in Egypt and Syria towards the end of the 1970s.

An evasion strategy used by several pathogens to avoid the innate immune system is to hide within the cells of their host (also called intracellular pathogenesis). Here, a pathogen spends most of its life-cycle inside host cells, where it is shielded from direct contact with immune cells, antibodies and complement. Some examples of intracellular pathogens include viruses, the food poisoning bacterium Salmonella and the eukaryotic parasites that cause malaria (Plasmodium falciparum) and leishmaniasis (Leishmania spp.). The intracellular lifestyle of a pathogen makes it challenging for the host not only to be infected, but to be cleared from the infection as its immune system can no longer reach it. The innate immune system is the first line of defense to infection and relies on the recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), which occur on surfaces of the invading microorganism or following their entry into the host cell. PAMPs serve as "signals" for various innate immune mechanisms including pathogen recognition receptors (PRRs), which activate signaling pathways that promote the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, as well as type I interferons (IFNs).

Intracellular pathogens may have evolved their mechanism not only to protect themselves from the cell damaging effects of the immune response, but also to take advantage of the immune response itself to their benefit. For instance, certain intracellular parasites take advantage of immune cells within their host to promote viral replication, whereas other mechanisms have been proposed to subvert an appropriate immune response that would prevent the development of an intracellular infection.

Both innate and adaptive immunity depend on the ability of the immune system to distinguish between self and non-self molecules. In immunology, self molecules are those components of an organism's body that can be distinguished from foreign substances by the immune system. Conversely, non-self molecules are those recognized as foreign molecules. T-cell activation and differentiation is triggered, in part, by recognition of specific non-self antigenic molecules on the surfaces of cell targets. Such activation can result, inter alia, in proliferation of activated T-cells and secretion of lymphokines, including cytokines. The cytokines so produced are the mediators of the immune response.
There are several well-known classes of cytokines: interleukins, for example interleukins 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6; lymphotoxins, examples of which are lymphotoxin-α and TNF-α; interferons, for example interferons α and β, interferons γ, interferon-τ, interferon-δ and interleukin-10. In addition, a number of other factors, e.g., tumor necrosis factor, platelet derived growth factor and transforming growth factor, have been identified that can mediate many facets of the immune response.
Dysregulation of the immune response has been implicated in the pathogenesis of numerous disease states. Such conditions range from autoimmune and inflammatory diseases to infectious conditions. Thus, modulation or suppression of the immune response can be an effective method for down-regulating a patient's immune system

The solubility of oxygen in water is temperature-dependent, and about twice as much (14.6 mg·L−1) dissolves at 0 °C than at 20 °C (7.6 mg·L−1). The majority of oxygen in the open atmosphere is molecular oxygen, but a certain percentage of molecular oxygen is photochemically transformed into other chemical species that are reactive with life.

Steam engines are external combustion engines, where the working fluid is separate from the combustion products. Two basic types of steam engines are the low pressure, closed system and the open, external combustion engine where the boiler is the sole source of the heat for the working fluid rather than an external heat source. As well a separate water-steam machine, the steam engine is the forerunner of the diesel engine.

A steam engine requires heat, steam and water. The heat is provided by a source external to the working fluid (steam) which results in the vaporization and the superheating of a large portion of the water. The steam which is the working fluid must be very hot (300–400 degrees Celsius). The pressure and volume of the steam is very small and as such the high pressure working fluid has to be expanded using a series of fixed orificed cylinders called the "expander". The engine exhaust is cooled in the process, which produces high temperature condensate. This water is recycled to be steam re-heated.
The open, external combustion, steam engine, where the boiler is the sole source of heat is not restricted by heat conduction unlike the closed steam engine.

History
The first steam engine is usually attributed to Leonardo da Vinci, or to Englishman John Smeaton. It involved a pair of counter-rotating paddles, which are driven by water jets, similar to a water wheel. John Smeaton's engine was built in 1695.

In addition to arguing that the rat population was insufficient to account for a bubonic plague pandemic, sceptics of the bubonic plague theory point out that the symptoms of the Black Death are not unique (and arguably in some accounts may differ from bubonic plague); that transference via fleas in goods was likely to be of marginal significance; and that the DNA results may be flawed and might not have been repeated elsewhere, despite extensive samples from other mass graves. Other arguments include the lack of accounts of the death of rats before outbreaks of plague between the 14th and 17th centuries; temperatures that are too cold in northern Europe for the survival of fleas; that, despite primitive transport systems, the spread of the Black Death was much faster than that of modern bubonic plague; that mortality rates of the Black Death appear to be very high; that, while modern bubonic plague is largely endemic as a rural disease, the Black Death indiscriminately struck urban and rural areas; and that the pattern of the Black Death, with major outbreaks in the same areas separated by 5 to 15 years, differs from modern bubonic plague—which often becomes endemic for decades with annual flare-ups.

Like sponges and cnidarians, ctenophores have two main layers of cells that sandwich a middle layer of jelly-like material, which is called the mesoglea in cnidarians and ctenophores; more complex animals have three main cell layers and no intermediate jelly-like layer. Hence ctenophores and cnidarians have traditionally been labelled diploblastic, along with sponges. Both ctenophores and cnidarians have a type of muscle that, in more complex animals, arises from the middle cell layer, and as a result some recent text books classify ctenophores as triploblastic, while others still regard them as diploblastic.

The traditional view of evolution of sponges and cnidarians and a slightly better view of early bilateria have been supported by molecular data. However, the exact order of evolution of bilateria is one that evolutionary biologists have been unable to resolve because of the lack of data from basal eumetazoan groups. Recently, molecular studies of ctenophores have started to shed light on the evolutionary relationships of Ctenophora.

An interesting feature of ctenophores is a ring of cilia around its oral aperture, called a cirral band, that moves in a circle to capture small particles of seawater, then releases them. This is thought to provide a mechanism for the evolution of a filter feeding stomach. The anatomy of ctenophore anatomy of the body is very unusual; there is only one oral aperture, the pharynx, at one end of an extremely elongate body and the anus at the opposite end (see Fig. 4.17a). The nervous system is more complex than in sponges and cnidarians and there are ganglia along the length of the body.

The Romans kept eight legions in five bases along the Rhine. The actual number of legions present at any base or in all, depended on whether a state or threat of war existed. Between about AD 14 and 180, the assignment of legions was as follows: for the army of Germania Inferior, two legions at Vetera (Xanten), I Germanica and XX Valeria (Pannonian troops); two legions at oppidum Ubiorum ("town of the Ubii"), which was renamed to Colonia Agrippina, descending to Cologne, V Alaudae, a Celtic legion recruited from Gallia Narbonensis and XXI, possibly a Galatian legion from the other side of the empire.

In a period of five to six hundred years, the base at Vetera is described as one of the longest-lived, continuously maintained, strategic military facilities in ancient history. It was continuously occupied from about 40 BC to AD 260. It was located at the confluence of the Rhine and the Lech Rivers, an excellent defensive position.

It was home to the main Roman military base for the time. The Rhine, flowing westward, provided transportation, water and an obstacle to enemies. The Lech and Rhöder Rivers provided additional transportation, and the location was chosen by Julius Caesar to build a small fortification that gave him additional defensive capabilities.

Under Vespasian, the fort was expanded to a full legionary base. By that time, the army of Germania Inferior included four legions. The first major change to the base occurred prior to Vespasian's time, under Augustus, when a new legion (XXXII) was established by transferring a cohort from II, that was now in Britannia. With the arrival of Vespasian, the base was further expanded and was made into headquarters of the commander of the Germania Inferior during the Third Roman Civil War (69–70). The base was again expanded in the second century by the construction of an additional auxiliary headquarters for four cohorts.

During the third century, additional garrisons were stationed at Vetera. After the third century, the base was used regularly, but was at various times the headquarters of a single legion or multiple legions. The surplus labour employed within the capitalist production process is only a temporary one, as the whole of that surplus labour is immediately employed in the production of new values [...] This is the source from which both the production and the exchange values of all commodities are derived. John Dalton's original atomic hypothesis assumed that all elements were monatomic and that the atoms in compounds would normally have the simplest atomic ratios with respect to one another. For example, Dalton assumed that water's formula was HO, giving the atomic mass of oxygen as 8 times that of hydrogen, instead of the modern value of about 16. When he found that this value was not consistent with known experimental data, he postulated a compound form of oxygen with a formula of (H2O)4. This "molecule" was based on Dalton's understanding of monatomic theory. The assumption of monatomic elements was abandoned after Robert Burns Lawler (1869) discovered that the ratios of chlorine atoms to hydrogen atoms and carbon atoms to nitrogen atoms in several compounds differed from the atomic ratios. In later theoretical work, it was accepted by J.J. Thomson that molecules are composed of atoms which are bonded to each other under certain circumstances.

Bonding
If a monatomic atom loses, say, one electron, it becomes a positive ion, and its ionic radius will be decreased (from about 0.836 to 0.835). As the negative charge of the electron becomes part of the nuclei of the atoms in the molecule, bonds will be formed between atoms having a net positive charge. Thus, the bonds between atoms in a molecule is called covalent bond(s) in chemistry and a bond between one monatomic atom to another is called a dative bond(s). Most work has been done on the spread of the plague in England, and even estimates of overall population at the start vary by over 100% as no census was undertaken between the time of publication of the Domesday Book and the year 1377. Population figures before 1360 are only known from church taxation records, which are often inadequate. A better alternative is to use the birth and death records preserved in parish registers. Estimating the Plague Mortality Rate 
There are many methods used to estimate the mortality rate of the plague. Some of the most common include:

Estimating the incidence and prevalence of the disease by calculating the number of deaths and the number of cases. Prevalence is calculated as the number of cases over a given period of time. Incidence is the same as prevalence but over a given period.
Estimating a proportion of the population who have an increased chance of dying at greater than the proportion among those who live healthy lives.

The principle of faunal succession is based on the appearance of fossils in sedimentary rocks. As organisms exist at the same time period throughout the world, their presence or (sometimes) absence may be used to provide a relative age of the formations in which they are found. Based on principles laid out by William Smith almost a hundred years before the publication of Charles Darwin's theory of evolution, the principles of succession were developed independently of evolutionary thought.  However, the similarities in the evidence suggested by Darwin would have been readily apparent to Smith, and is now recognized as an example of convergent evolution. However, some authors state that it was Charles Lyell who first suggested using the principles of succession to estimate relative ages of rocks.

Faunal succession refers to the process of rock formation through the time of the life history of organisms of a species, so that faunas from older rocks are overlaid by those from younger rocks.  Thus it may be used to determine the relative positions of successive strata deposited on the floor of the ancient oceans.

In the United States 

In the United States, the principle was first used to determine the relative age of the stratigraphical units in western states by geologists working in the second half of the 19th century. In 1891 Scottish chemist James Dewar was able to produce enough liquid oxygen to study. The first commercially viable process for producing liquid oxygen was independently developed in 1895 by German engineer Carl von Linde and British engineer William Hampson. Both men lowered the temperature of air until it liquefied and then distilled the component gases by boiling them off one at a time and capturing them.

The technology used to make liquid oxygen is not as useful for atmospheric cooling as for industrial processes. That didn’t prevent its earliest adopters, including James Dewar, from producing other high-pressure gases and other products useful in industry at the time. In the first years of the 20th century chemical engineers were using compressed oxygen to clean out steelmaking furnaces, as oxygen is more effective at melting iron at high pressures than are other gaseous oxidizers like air.

While some have claimed Dewar’s first liquid oxygen production was in the laboratory of his London physics department colleagues E. Armstrong and W. Ramsay, that couldn’t be further from the truth. Dewar’s first success was in the physics laboratory of William Thomson at University College London, just four hundred yards from his laboratory at University College. In 1891 Thomson had designed a liquid pump to move air-gas mixtures such as air-fuel mixtures and steam-gases. Lake Constance consists of three bodies of water: the Obersee ("upper lake"), the Untersee ("lower lake"), and a connecting stretch of the Rhine, called the Seerhein ("Lake Rhine"). The lake is situated in Germany, Switzerland and Austria near the Alps. Specifically, its shorelines lie in the German states of Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, the Austrian state of Vorarlberg, and the Swiss cantons of Thurgau and St. Gallen.

The lake is the largest lake in the Alps and a major international border crossing; a bridge connects Austria and Switzerland at the lakeside village of Friedrichshafen. At the shore of the lake are the border crossings of Bruck/Mur and Währing/Unterwasser between Germany and Austria, and St. Valentin between Germany and Switzerland.

Climate
Lake Constance is a small temperate lake bordered by steep mountains. Consequently, the climate is moderate, with warm summers and cold, snowy winters.  Average high temperatures in July range from around 16 °C (60 °F) to 30 °C (86 °F), but the record warm temperature for July is 45.9 °C (113 °F), which was measured by a weather station on 25 August 2018. Average high temperatures in January hover around 2 °C (mid-30s Fahrenheit), with the record low temperature being −32.4 °C (−22 °F), recorded in July 1933. Precipitation is abundant, amounting to 2,950 mm (116 inches) annually. This makes the lake a perfect location for bathing and fishing.

Geography
The western shore lies in the lowlands of Germany's Württembergische Schweiz (Upper Swabia). The southern shore of Constance is located in Austria. Constance lies in the Southern Alps, a mountain chain in the eastern Austrian state of Vorarlberg and west-central-southern-northern Switzerland. By Jennifer C. GravelleThis paper reviews the current evidence on the incidence of the corporate tax from Harberger-type general equilibrium models, with special attention to the open economy. The analysis identifies the major drivers of the results from open-economy models and compares estimates from four major studies that have examined corporate tax incidence in an open economy. The studies vary in the assumptions of critical elasticities, and the variations account for differences in the reported estimates. Overall, we find evidence suggesting that the major determinants of the estimates are the estimated elasticity of demand with respect to corporate taxation and the assumption about the marginal cost of corporate taxes.

1. Overview of the Literature

The literature to evaluate the tax incidence literature (i.e., the empirical evidence of the channels through which the corporate tax influences economic welfare) has focused on two fundamental research areas. The first research area is the study of a firm's profitability, and the second studies the impact of taxation on firm demand and investment. The literature can be divided along these two lines, with each line drawing on empirical or theoretical literature as well as data to inform the analysis. With respect to the theoretical literature, the main approach for analyzing the channels through which the corporate tax affects the economy is to use an open-economy general equilibrium model. The open-economy models typically incorporate a trade model, a production model, and a microeconomic model for the effects of the corporate tax on the firm's profitability. Microorganisms or toxins that successfully enter an organism encounter the cells and mechanisms of the innate immune system. The innate response is usually triggered when microbes are identified by pattern recognition receptors, which recognize components that are conserved among broad groups of microorganisms, or when damaged, injured or stressed cells send out alarm signals, many of which (but not all) are recognized by the same receptors as those that recognize pathogens. The detection of microorganisms/toxins by receptors on cells in the innate immune system stimulates the expression of a series of downstream intracellular molecules and triggers defense responses in the cells, including the expression of proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines and antimicrobial peptides. Pattern recognition receptors have broad functional similarities but show marked differences in their selectivity to different microorganisms and the response to pathogenic stimuli differ depending on cell type and on cell type. Generally, cells of adaptive immunity, such as those in the T- and B-cell compartment are activated by specific antigens. Cells of the innate immune system do not need this specific recognition to trigger a pathogen attack. Moreover, adaptive response is typically limited to one type of cell while innate immunity is usually widespread.

A subset of pattern recognition receptors called C-type lectins plays a specialized role in a wide range of cellular defense systems, including antimicrobial defenses, by binding to bacterial, viral and fungal glycoconjugates [@R1]--[@R3]. Paleoclimatologists measure the ratio of oxygen-18 and oxygen-16 in the shells and skeletons of marine organisms to determine what the climate was like millions of years ago (see oxygen isotope ratio cycle). Seawater molecules that contain the lighter isotope, oxygen-16, evaporate at a slightly faster rate than water molecules containing the 12% heavier oxygen-18; this disparity increases at lower temperatures. During periods of lower global temperatures, snow and rain from that evaporated water tends to be higher in oxygen-16, and the seawater left behind tends to be higher in oxygen-18.

When a large body of warm water displaces the cooler water in the depths, the heavier oxygen-18 that gets concentrated in the displaced water finds its way to the upper levels of the ocean. Such a process lowers the O-16/O-18 ratio and creates an "apparent anomaly" because the global average O-16/O-18 ratio is normally 16%. Thus a low 18O-to-16O ratio is evidence for a period of greater warmth than the present. O-16 shows up in the shells of corals and mollusk shells and in living planktonic organisms like foraminifera (protozoa) and pteropods.

O-16/O-18 in the deep

The annual cycle of solar activity is responsible for altering the ocean's oxygen content. In the northern Pacific Ocean, for example, in the months following a new cycle of solar activity, atmospheric pressure increases and cloud cover decreases in the eastern Pacific, allowing solar radiation and low clouds to penetrate more deeply into the ocean. As a result, in the months of September to November, seawater in the upper ocean becomes slightly enriched in the heavier isotope (the 18O-to-16O ratio in the ocean rises).

The 18O/16O cycle is so slow it cannot be measured directly but can be inferred from other parameters, such as atmospheric pressure and the ocean temperature. The 18O/16O ratio of seawater can be measured in the ocean deep, where for a variety of reasons the surface water has a different isotopic composition, and a difference in 18O/16O is expected. According to the Standard Atmosphere Model the ratio should in fact rise with depth, and indeed this is the case.

Geochronology is a non intrusive, relatively cheap method of dating the crust and upper mantle of continents and most of Earth's lithosphere. It provides a timeline of mineral deposition, with a resolution of less than 2,000 years in many cases. It measures many isotopic ratios in minerals that can be linked to age. In humans, this response is activated by complement binding to antibodies that have attached to these microbes or the binding of complement proteins to carbohydrates on the surfaces of microbes. This recognition signal triggers a rapid killing response. The speed of the response is a result of signal amplification that occurs following sequential proteolytic activation of complement molecules, which are also proteases. Upon activation, complement is considered a protease that activates downstream cascades in a sequential manner, resulting in attack by three major pathways ([@B1]): (1) the classical pathway, (2) the alternative pathway, and (3) the membrane attack pathway.

Although complement is an effective defense against pathogenic microbes, activation of complement can lead to anaphylaxis. Patients with immune system deficiencies, such as those with nephritic syndromes that can cause complement dysregulation, are more prone to developing anaphylactic reactions upon antibiotic therapy ([@B1], [@B2]). Thus, a delicate balance must be maintained to allow for effective defenses against infectious agents while still preventing autoimmunity. The human body has several regulatory mechanisms that prevent this uncontrolled immune hyperactivity ([@B2]). These mechanisms include soluble and cellular forms of inhibitors within each pathway, the inhibition of complement activation by antibodies that attach to the surface of cells or by competing for common C3 convertase enzymes, as well as complement receptor blockage. A recent study by Zhang and colleagues provides evidence that the immune response to the oral pathogen *Candida albicans* is strongly regulated by the complement system and, in part, by soluble receptors that prevent self-recognition. Scm is a benign fibroblastic lesion which usually occurs in newborns with high clinical and pathological resemblance to rhabdomyosarcoma. Diabetic myonecrosis is an insidious but underreported complication of insulin dependent diabetes mellitus which occurs frequently as a complication of poorly - controlled diabetes mellitus \[[@B1]--[@B3]\]. The chao was made of paper pulp made from mulberry tree bark fibers, which is why it has the reddish tinge. The paper was made using a technique of pressing the paper, rather than applying it on a surface to adhere to a surface in a manner similar to the way that modern paper is made. The first paper currencies in China appeared soon after.

After the Yuan was replaced by the Ming in 1368, chao was used as a general term, not just a currency. It then reappeared during the early Qing dynasty, when it was printed in copper or aluminum.

While the Chinese currency was one of the first to use this modern technology, it was not the first by far. This was made possible by the technology found in the Chinese coin and stamp manufacturing, where Chinese coins were used as a mold to print paper currency. Inflammation is produced by eicosanoids and cytokines, which are released by injured or infected cells. Once released, these mediators cause local inflammation.
During inflammation tissue-damaging enzymes are released into body fluids, including blood serum. These enzymes, or other components, play a role in diseases such as burns and wounds. One such enzyme found in blood during inflammation is the creatine kinase-NSE (EC 2.7.3.2) isoenzyme, which occurs naturally in the brain or nervous system and in the testicles of males, or in the ovaries and placenta of females.
Several isoforms of creatine kinase exist in blood resulting from multiple sources including muscle tissue, brain tissue, and liver tissue. Creatine kinase (CK) isoenzymes are found throughout the body, and at least ten isoenzymes of creatine kinase have been detected in mammals thus far. Creatine kinase is most often associated with the movement of energy within cells. Two of the most prominent members of the enzyme family are creatine kinase BB (e.g., creatine kinase type II isoform B) and creatine kinase MB (e.g., creatino kinase type II isoform M), also known as creatine kinase B-type (EC 2.7.3.2) and creatine kinase M-type (EC 2.7.3.2), respectively.

Many theories have been suggested in immunology from the end of the nineteenth century up to the present time. The end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century saw a battle between "cellular" and "humoral" theories of immunity. In the 1930s the "tumor-immunity association" hypothesis was formulated by Ehrlich. Based upon the presence of antibodies in cancer patients, the theory was that tumors induce their own destruction by generating antibodies against cell proteins. A prime number (or a prime) is a natural number greater than 1 that has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself. By extension, any number composed of a prime number and a non-prime number is a composite number. A composite number is therefore a natural number greater than 1 composed of two or more positive integers, but not including 1  (1 being the positive integer less than -1 ). In the natural numbers, there are infinitely many prime numbers.

Etymology

In the early 17th-century, the word prime began as the noun for "primeval ancestor," deriving from the Latin primus "the first" and probably influenced by the Old French prim, meaning "prize," from the Proto-Indo-European root pḱr- "foremost." The Old English for "prime" (noun or noun proper) was prīm, and in Middle English primme; this meant "first" or "principal." It was through the change of the final part of prīm, -me, into -re, -um, -um, that the modern form prīm- became common.

This molecule resembles a subset of immunoglobulins and is encoded by an unusual gene with atypical features, including the presence of several tandem variable domains followed by a single constant domain, a transmembrane domain, and an intracellular signaling domain. The molecular characteristics of these molecules define a novel class of immunoglobulins termed "natural antibodies" that were discovered more than 25 years ago and have been assumed to be encoded by germline-determined genes. The plague disease, caused by Yersinia pestis, is enzootic (commonly present) in populations of fleas carried by ground rodents, including marmots, in various areas including Central Asia, Kurdistan, Western Asia, Northern India and Uganda. Nestorian graves dating to 1338–39 near Lake Issyk Kul in Kyrgyzstan have inscriptions referring to plague and are thought by many epidemiologists to mark the outbreak of the epidemic, from which it could easily have spread to China and India. In October 2010, medical geneticists suggested that all three of the great waves of the plague originated in China.

In Asia, the disease was first recorded in 1822 and the first large outbreaks were in China in 1855–59 and again in 1860. In 1894–1895, the plague appeared in India. A large outbreak of the disease affected millions of people in India and China in the 1860s. In 1917–1918, in China, a major epidemic of rat-carried bubonic plague occurred, causing the deaths of about 3,000,000 people and leading to the deaths of 7,000,000 more from famine and malnutrition. The plague appeared in the Philippines for the first time in 1909 and had remained an endemic disease in the country since then. During the 1910s-1920s, epidemics occurred in different parts of the country with several large outbreaks in the first decade of 21st century.

The United States was not an initial victim of plague during the great plague epidemic of 1894–1896. Despite outbreaks in the early 1890s, the U.S. plague record is relatively sparse, suggesting that the plague was already extinct in the United States by the early 20th century.

The first recorded case of plague in America occurred in Louisiana in November 1894, followed by a massive outbreak of the disease in San Joaquin County

text: osteoporotic vertebral fractures are associated with considerable reduction of quality of life , morbidity , and mortality . This has implications for patients, for payers and regulators, and for society in general. However, in spite of major advances in understanding of the mechanisms leading to vertebral fracture, and of the effectiveness of non-operative treatment (e.g., pharmacotherapy and non-opioid analgesics) vertebral fracture is still poorly managed on a primary or secondary level. In most countries, osteoporotic and non-osteoporotic vertebral fractures are still not included in major health insurance coverage. In the United States, reimbursement for non-surgical management of vertebral fractures is available only for osteoporotic fractures, and may be partial for other fractures. In Europe, reimbursement of non-operative therapy is more extensive, with a stronger tendency on the health insurance sides towards treatment for all fractures, including osteoporotic fractures. This review describes the clinical impact of vertebral fractures, their prevention, and current efforts to improve outcomes. We also discuss recent developments in the understanding of fracture pathophysiology, identify challenges for the future, and suggest steps as to how to increase the awareness of the major impact of vertebral fractures and promote better treatment.

Deforestation is the conversion of forested areas to non-forested areas. The main sources of deforestation in the Amazon are human settlement and development of the land. Prior to the early 1960s, access to the forest's interior was highly restricted, and the forest remained basically intact.
The destruction, degradation and removal of forest cover have adverse environmental effects such as: loss of biodiversity; loss of vital hydrological flow and loss of the ecosystem services (e.g., nutrient flow from decaying biomass to water; water filtration and purification; erosion protection; carbon sequestration), all of which contribute significantly to global climate change.
Forest cover has also traditionally been a source of wood for the construction industry. Deforestation may substantially diminish the supply of wood to the construction industry. Forest clearance is required to make way for housing developments, roads, railways tracks, dams such as hydroelectric power plants, dams for large cities, etc.
The primary source of income for developing countries is agriculture, particularly forest products (e.g., timber, fruit, and rubber). The rate of forest degradation is the product of human population density and per capita consumption demand, as well as the technical efficiency of economic activities and the level of industrialization.
Many different methods have been employed to preserve, restore and/or regenerate forested areas throughout history. The following are some of the more common approaches employed today.

Since all modern ctenophores except the beroids have cydippid-like larvae, it has widely been assumed that their last common ancestor also resembled cydippids, having an egg-shaped body and a pair of retractable tentacles. Richard Harbison's purely morphological analysis in 1985 concluded that the cydippids are not monophyletic, in other words do not contain all and only the descendants of a single common ancestor that was itself a cydippid. Instead he found that various cydippid families were more similar to members of other ctenophore orders than to other cydippids. However, this analysis did not address the evolutionary relationship between embryos and adult ctenophores.

Recently the first molecular phylogenies of ctenophores were published, based on the mitochondrial 16S ribosomal DNA (rDNA), the nuclear 18S rDNA, and the 28S nuclear rDNA [@pone.0110769-Vacelet1]--[@pone.0110769-Vacelet3]. These phylogenies showed that the morphologically simple larvae can be divided into several distinct groups, all of them clearly related to adult ctenophores. The larvacean and beroid suborders are thus two independent clades. The phylogenetic relationships between these groups of larvae remain largely unresolved. The weight of boilers and condensers generally makes the power-to-weight ratio of a steam plant lower than for internal combustion engines. For mobile applications steam has been largely superseded by internal combustion engines or electric motors.

External combustion 
External power sources generate the internal heat by burning fuel (gasoline, diesel etc.) to create combustion heat. Water heaters may use the same heat transfer element as hot-water boilers but are not usually as efficient as these. Fuel consumption is higher and the power-to-weight ratio is reduced.

Thermal oil 
Thermal oil boilers usually use a circulating oil. Fuel can be burned to produce combustion hot, after which the hot oil (usually oil-gasoline emulsion) is pumped through heat exchangers and heated again, using part of the heat to warm the exhaust gases, to warm the cold water circulating through the plant by evaporating it into steam in a closed system, using the rest of the heat to heat water. The steam leaves the boiler through condensers and the hot water is heated in exchangers. When the thermal oil reaches the upper stages of the boiler (mainly where the temperature is reduced), oil is converted into gas and combusted again in a furnace to obtain heat. The heating of the engine and of its oil has the same thermal effect as the "cold start" of an internal combustion engine without starting. The process requires a considerable number of valves and safety systems.

Hot water 
A water boiler is a device that heats water using the combustion of some other fuel than the water. The heat is dissipated by means of transferring the heat to the water contained in the boiler by either boiling the water or heating it with steam. The heating of the water raises its temperature above the surrounding temperature of air or a different fluid and makes it useful and usable for a variety of tasks that are not possible with water at a constant temperature. For that to occur, there must be at least two temperatures, the temperature of the water and that of the air or other fluid that surrounds the water.

Seismologists can use the arrival times of seismic waves in reverse to image the interior of the Earth. This is known as seismology. Most important for seismologists are seismic waves generated in the Earth’s upper mantle located at depths of several hundred kilometers to a several thousands of kilometers below the surface. These waves travel at velocities of a few kilometers per second to the uppermost part of the mantle about 400 kilometers below the surface. Then they go through a transition zone called the ‘ductile-deformation zone’, which is a region where strong compaction of the material causes a decrease in velocity. This leads to waves with significantly smaller velocities that enter the lower mantle. Those waves move in a relatively short distance (usually of the order of 10’s of kilometers) to where they are detected by our instruments, either on the surface or on land, or buried on ships, or in the ocean.
To make maps of the velocities of these waves, seismologists use so-called ‘wave-forms’. These are records of the waves recorded as a function of time.
These wave-forms are then analysed using well-known Fourier methods to obtain information about the waves of different frequencies in which they are travelling. In the Earth, these waves contain the information of the depth of the source of the waves, and the velocity and location at or near the surface of the wave. In 1971 Roberts and AT&T's president John deCarlo partnered in Telenet and won a contract for an IPX-protocol-based network to run on a portion of the ARPANET network backbone. On January 4, 1972, the company started offering a 24x7 ARPANET access service by leasing time on the network to university investigators. The service was based entirely on time-sharing, where access was restricted to users who paid a monthly charge.

As it grew to serve a larger user community, Telenet found itself the target of controversy. As the company grew to hundreds of users a day, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) became concerned that the size of the service posed a "potential abuse to the network". This creates three main flows, two of which change names rather often. The largest and southern main branch begins as Waal and continues as Boven Merwede ("Upper Merwede"), Beneden Merwede ("Lower Merwede"), Noord River ("North River"), Nieuwe Maas ("New Meuse"), Het Scheur ("the Rip") and Nieuwe Waterweg ("New Waterway"). The second main branch, that of the IJssel begins as Nederrijn and continues as IJssel. The third and smallest branch begins at the confluence of the Boven Merwede and Nederrijn and continues as Lijn and Ij into the North Sea.

The Rhine Delta is located west and north of the Maas Delta. To the east the delta is bordered by the North Sea and to the west it is bordered by the IJsselmeer. The Maas and Rhine form two branches of the Rhine as they enter the North Sea. These two channels form the main channel which flows from south to north. The centrifugal governor was adopted by James Watt for use on a steam engine in 1788 after Watt’s partner Boulton saw one at a flour mill Boulton & Watt were building. The governor could not actually hold a set speed, because it would assume a new constant speed in response to load changes. The governor was able to handle smaller variations such as those caused by fluctuating heat load to the boiler.

During the nineteenth and early 20th century, a number of automatic control systems were developed. The first was the vacuum governor, invented by Ewart Evans in 1874.[1] A vacuum was established in the governor's primary chamber by opening a series of valves, which increased the speed at which the motion of the diaphragm was transferred to the control chamber, which in turn increased the closing force on the control lever. This was used to regulate the main (solenoid) valve, and therefore engine speed. There were many limitations to the use of vacuum governors for the control of prime mover operation, since they were prone to seizing or binding if not sufficiently lubricated. Also, vacuum governors of the time could not withstand frequent start-stop cyclic variations such as occurred in passenger transport. Also, vacuum governors could not produce rapid speed adjustments when load was changed. This lack of rapid response would prevent vacuum governors from being feasible for use in the modern auto

Natural killer cells, or NK cells, are a component of the innate immune system which does not directly attack invading microbes. Rather, NK cells destroy compromised host cells, such as tumor cells or virus-infected cells, recognizing such cells by a condition known as "missing self." This term describes cells with low levels of a cell-surface marker called MHC I (major histocompatibility complex) – a situation that can arise in viral infections of host cells. NK cells kill these so-called nonself cells by releasing cytotoxic granules that contain granzymes, serine proteases and perforin that digest the target cell, and by directly lysing the cell. In some instances, NK cell cytotoxicity requires a "licensing" interaction between a cell surface receptor on NK cells (NKG2D) and MHC class I molecules expressed on target cells.

NK cells are thought to originate in the bone marrow where they undergo extensive selection and maturation by antigen on bone marrow-derived lymphoid tissues.

As NK cells are activated by viral infections, they will be the first cells to be activated by the viral antigens. Once activated, NK-cells will proliferate and produce many cytotoxic molecules such as perforin, granzymes and cytokines, such as interferon.

Functions 
The primary functions of NK cells are the suppression of autoreactive T-cells and the protection of the fetus from paternal attack by transplacentation. They do not recognize MHC I self molecules.  They are involved in innate immunity, and are involved in regulating the activities of other immune cells such as T, B lymphocytes, and dendritic cells. NK cells are the primary effector cell for immune attack on viruses and tumors; they are important for protecting the fetus from attack by the mother's immune cells, including NK cells, and in the early control of viral infections before the T cell mediated immune responses become activated. The most basic method of checking the primality of a given integer n is called trial division. Here's how to do it:

Take a prime factor p, try dividing n by it, if n is divided evenly, then no prime factor is left. But if the new remainder was smaller than half of n, then p is still a factor of n. Go back to the next factor of p and repeat. In the above example, we might say that 2 is a factor of 3, so we'll try dividing by it, and we'll find that we get 3. 6 divides evenly into 11, and therefore 2 is not a factor.
But of course, we want to check as many values as we can in a time period that won't take forever, so we keep a count of how many times we're trying divisibility for a given factor, and once it's reached a certain number, we give up and return false.

This is the most well-known algorithm, but many people don't realize that it was not the first way to check primality.

This "Chinese" method for checking primality was the first efficient way. It goes like this:

Divide the given integer by each prime up to the square root of n. Keep track of each divisor as you go, and if you get back to 1, then the integer is a prime.

The Scotland Act 1998, which was passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom and given royal assent by Queen Elizabeth II on 19 November 1998, governs the functions and role of the Scottish Parliament and delimits its legislative competence. The Scotland Act 2012 extends the devolved competencies. For the purposes of parliamentary sovereignty, the Parliament of the United Kingdom at Westminster continues to constitute the supreme legislature of Scotland.

In line with the Edinburgh Agreement of 1993[1], Scottish citizens were represented in the parliament by a single Member of Parliament for each of Scotland's constituencies.

History

The original Scottish Parliament consisted of a chamber or house, with its members known as members of the House of Commons, and a separate house called the Lords, with its members called members of the House of Lords. In the House of Lords there was a Scottish Peerage, consisting of a number of ancient earldoms and baronies. Scottish representatives and peers were chosen by the Crown, and were entitled to sit in the House of Lords on a personal basis. Members of the Scottish Parliament took their seats according to the number of votes in the Scottish constituencies and were not permitted any control of the proceedings of the House of Lords.

In 1998, the House of Lords was abolished, thereby creating the current system of a single member elected by the Scottish Constituency in the People's House with a supplementary member nominated by the Scottish Parliament's Leader of the House of Lords to represent the interests of the Scottish peers.

The Westminster Parliament also has legislative power with the remainder being reserved for the governments of England and Northern Ireland, which cannot veto the Scottish Parliament's legislative plans.

As a result of the Scotland Act 1998, the Parliament's initial legislative programme included areas of devolved competence relating to agriculture, communications and broadcasting, cultural affairs, education, the environment and transport and the economy. In practice, the devolved areas of competence have since been enlarged significantly. In areas covered by the Scottish Parliament there have been further devolution schemes as new issues have arisen.

Structure

Members of the Parliament are directly elected under the first-past-the-post system from 29 districts called constituencies. The constituency members are then organised into the Parliament's two chambers.

Lobates have eight comb-rows, originating at the aboral pole and usually not extending beyond the body to the lobes; in species with (four) auricles, the cilia edging the auricles are extensions of cilia in four of the comb rows. Most lobates are quite passive when moving through the water, using the cilia on their comb rows for propulsion, although Leucothea has long and active auricles whose movements also contribute to propulsion. The eight comb rows on the body are long and unbranched; in species without lobate-combs on the sides, the rows on the tail are short and unbranched. There are usually at least two auricles located on the aboral side of the body; and there may be additional auricles on the ventral surface. There are either five (Leucothea, Pterocella) to seven (Leptonema) pharyngeal pores, arranged in two opposing rows; two on the dorsal side, two on the ventral side, and two on the aboral-lobate pole. All eight dorsal-lobe and six of the aboral-lobate pores have a row of papillae on their ventral face, forming what are called the papillae of the mouth. As a country develops, it acquires more capital, which leads to the owners of this capital having more wealth and income and introducing inequality.

this article introduces a highly parallel algorithm for molecular dynamics simulations with short - range forces on single node multi- and many - core systems . the algorithm is designed to achieve high parallel speedups for strongly inhomogeneous systems like nanodevices or nanostructured materials . The algorithm is an extension of parallel simplex searches on the atomic level, which uses many cores to speed up a short - range contact model while keeping the overall CPU time nearly constant. A new scaling factor is introduced to define local atom velocities which allows to achieve high speedup factors even on systems with strongly varying load distribution.

Introduction

The recent development of new materials with nanometer-sized structures has triggered the development of powerful and user-friendly simulation packages such as GROMACS [1] or LAMMPS [2] to study the physical properties of such exotic materials. Many problems in structural biology or materials science arise, where the atomic structure of molecules is crucial when studying their function. One such process is an atomic or molecular motion governed by the Newton´s equation of motion and the laws of thermodynamics. Therefore, it is crucial to be able to evaluate forces and other related quantities acting on the atoms in order to compute the overall motion. To study such processes, it becomes a requirement to be able to study molecular dynamics simulations on a single machine or cluster of computers, since many important processes occur on sub-nanometer timescales. The most important physical quantities to quantify are forces. However, for many-core architectures, the evaluation of these forces becomes a computational challenge. In modern architectures, there may exist processors with more cores than those available to run the whole system in parallel. So the time step - defined as the time between two physics steps - must be adjusted to the speed of those cores as long as the overall CPU time remains constant. So, it might be impossible to simulate very short but very fast processes and therefore not possible to use any high performance processors.

Quicksort first chooses a pivot value, p, that comes between the smallest and largest elements in the list. For example, p could be the number one (1) in the example. For every element except the pivot, the algorithm compares it with p and places it right next to the one which has a greater value. For example, [3, 6, 2, 1, 4] is sorted as [3, 2, 1, 4, 6].
Then, if q is the number of elements in the list, the sorted list is [p, x, x, x, x]. Next, q - 1 elements are compared with p. Thus, after q-1 elements are used, the list is [p, x, x, x,..., p]. At this point, the algorithm is going to start comparing more elements with the p on its left side. At the left side there are the elements that start with p, plus the remaining previous elements.
The algorithm will repeat for the list, swapping some elements to their right until all elements in the list are either in the left or in the right.

I was looking forward to this so much, being a big fan of the book. However, when it came out I remember thinking it was one of the biggest wastes of money and time I've ever spent at the cinema.

In principle, the acting, the sets and the music were excellent, and are the main reason why I'm rating this a 4.

In this version, Sara is a little too self-sacrificing for my taste. There is no way she would have deliberately lied to Miss Minchin just to stop her punishing the other girls; in the book she makes a point of describing lies as ""not just wicked, but vulgar."" That's not to say that Sara isn't a sympathetic character, she's just not the manipulative shrew the show turned her into. Likewise, the other actresses didn't bring their A game to the screen.

As for the sets, they were beautiful. If I'd been given a choice between the book and this TV "adaptation", I would not have wasted my time and money on the latter.

The same applies to the music. The songs in the book are very varied and a joy to hear, in part because they have a more realistic rhythm to them compared to the music for the TV show. Again, for that reason this score was one of the best musical experiences I've had, but in this version it's mostly the same as the one sung in the play.
