Crohn's disease (CD) is a complex disorder resulting from the interaction of intestinal microbiota with the host immune system in genetically susceptible individuals. The largest meta-analysis of genome-wide association to date identified 71 CD–susceptibility loci in individuals of European ancestry. An important epidemiological feature of CD is that it is 2–4 times more prevalent among individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish (AJ) descent compared to non-Jewish Europeans (NJ). The incidence of CD among AJ patients is 20.8/100,000 per year compared to 6.9/100,000 per year among NJ patients, although the prevalence among individuals of Ashkenazi ancestry is approximately 100 times higher than the prevalence in NJ populations.

The most convincing explanation for this is that Ashkenazi Jewish individuals share several susceptibility alleles (‘multiple susceptibility alleles’) whose cumulative effect results in this phenotype. Identifying these alleles requires a more careful analysis of clinical and genetic factors which influence disease expression. To date, it is suggested that genetic contributions from the host interact with three key factors: genetic ancestry; the presence and density of pathogen-associated antigens; and the composition and function of the gut microbiota. The focus of this review is to describe the genetic contributions to CD which are of key importance in understanding the disease biology. Such studies have the potential to identify potential targets for personalized medicine for affected AJ patients.

Southern California consists of one of the more varied collections of geologic, topographic, and natural ecosystem landscapes in a diversity outnumbering other major regions in the state and country. The Pacific and Mojave Ranges meet the San Gabriel Valley and the San Bernardino Mountains, the desert reaches the Mediterranean climate of Greater Los Angeles, and the Sonoran Desert, with its unique flora and fauna, borders the Colorado River.

Much of the California landscape is a mosaic of geologic strata, old river valleys, and topographic terraces, interrupted by abrupt and complex rock formations.

Geology

The geology of Southern California is characterized by sedimentary rocks (chiefly sandstone and shale, overlain by hard igneous rocks as outcroppings), formed primarily in the early, middle, and late Cretaceous periods. During the Devonian Period (about 335 to 360 million years ago) the shallow-water, brackish-water regions, rich in plant life, were home to a wide variety of organisms similar to those found in modern-day saltwater swamps. During the next period, the Paleozoic, (about 375 to about 542 million years ago) the great oceans covered much of earth. Over millions of years, sediments deposited in the former shallow seas were subject to extreme pressures that pushed the rocks up from below, forming the mountains that are so important to the modern landscape in Southern California.

Geography

Southern California is a coastal plain in the coastal mountain region, which marks the southern end of the transverse mountain range extending northeast from the San Andreas Fault. The plain covers about 1,600 miles (2,500 km) in length from the San Diego-Baja California border to the Oregon border, averaging 100 miles (160 km) in width.

The development of plate tectonics provided a physical basis for many observations of the solid Earth. Long linear regions of geologic features could be explained as plate boundaries. Mid-ocean ridges, high regions on the seafloor where hydrothermal vents and volcanoes exist, were explained as divergent boundaries, where two plates move apart. Hot spots occur along convergent boundaries, where two plates move towards each others. The location of these hot spots as observed on a map of Earth was used to deduce where the plates are moving. These ideas were developed in the mid-twentieth century. However, before plate tectonic theory was developed, the movement of the plates was still viewed as magical. If you could move a rock on the seafloor or on the surface of the Earth, you might be able to move the earth on its axis, and to move the whole Earth on the axis, which would change where the sun and the other planets were located!

The work of Charles Richter, an American seismologist, led to an improved understanding of the relationship between earthquakes and volcanoes. In 1935 he published a famous paper in Nature in which he used the seismic waves that follow an earthquake, like a wake, to create an image of the shape of the Earth. The image he developed looked like a pancake with the pancake’s major axis normal to the Earth’s surface, its minor axis in the vertical direction, pointing vertically out of the plane of the pancake, and the pancake was flattened vertically by about 40 km. In this image the thickest crust is at the center of the pancake, and this part of the crust is where the strongest earthquakes occur. The depth of seismicity along a given fault is normally constant, so that the depth can be inferred from the amplitude of the earthquake. This technique allowed seismologists to understand better how the crust is distributed within the Earth, the crust at depth being much thicker than the surface.

These changes are referred to as changes of awareness. Awareness changes can be of either subjective or objective nature and depend on the frequency and intensity of the stimulus. If these changes are not taken into consideration, they may lead to misinterpretation of the tms response. Some examples of changes in awareness are light sensitivity, sound distortion, altered consciousness (, fear or euphoria and, in exceptional cases, even psychosis ) caused by stimulation in the same area or near the motor cortex. It is not exactly known whether these awareness changes are permanent or reversible. tms is a non-invasive procedure and does not require anesthesia or local or intravenous sedation. Near the end of the 19th century compound engines came into widespread use. These had a single firebox, enclosed by the locomotive frame, mounted on top of the locomotive driving axles. Typically, the fireboxes were constructed of cast iron in 3″ and 6″ long sections that were bolted to steel castings called "frames" with endcaps bolted on.

The first of the compound locomotives to be built were the German Nordhütte, based on the Prussian J.I.C. 4-2-2-2 compound built at Berlin-Rosi-Werke, the first compound locomotive of all European countries. The locomotives were built under the supervision of chief mechanical engineer, the father of the compound engine design, Gustav von Lindenthal, and chief builder and designer at Berlin-Rosi-Werke, Albert Gräveson. A total of nine J.I.C. compound locomotives were built at the Nordhütte.

A major advance for British compound locomotives took place with the Locomotive on a “Watt Principle”, or self-heating, and self-propagated, boiler.  The principle was used for several British compound engines. These were the North British, the Great Eastern and the “Tramway”, or Great Central. The compound locomotives were the largest to be designed and built in one factory in Britain and were the largest compound locomotives to run to that date. Compound construction revolutionized locomotives by giving a new level of efficiency, safety and performance.

You can no more be harassed by a mag than you can be assaulted by a TV show or beaten up by a film poster." If that's what you believe, then I'm afraid that I am going to have to convince you otherwise.

So why not assume that a magazine can be thrown around like a deadly dart, or beaten, for that matter, with a rubber hose, or smashed with a baseball bat, just in case? At the approach of its centennial, Saura drew together an unprecedented wealth of talent from the Spanish performing arts community to create this quintessential love song to their homeland. A regulation of the Rhine was called for, with an upper canal near Diepoldsau and a lower canal at Fußach, in order to counteract the constant flooding and strong sedimentation in the western Rhine Delta. A major obstacle in the implementation of this regulation was the Cologne-Höxter Railway Bridge, which stood right above the planned lower canal and was then considered as the highest bridge ever built.

However, the Cologne-Höxter Bridge was demolished without legal action on 20 May 1896.

On 20 September 1896, the Federal government approved the construction of the Rhine canal (as Rheintalbahn). The construction of the canal began in the summer of 1897.

The Rhine canal had a length of almost  and a width of. Its canalisation followed the course of the former Lower Left Rhine and the middle and lower right branches of the now defunct right side of the Middle Rhine. The Cologne-Höxter Railway Bridge was replaced by the   Cologne–Höxter Railway Bridge across the canal.

The Rhine Valley Railway Bridge, which was to cross the middle left branch of the Middle Rhine,  was not replaced, because a flood in 1899 had destroyed the bridge and the right-wing was blocked by sediment, so that no further transport traffic was possible. In the laboratory, stratigraphers analyze samples of stratigraphic sections that can be returned from the field, such as those from drill cores. Stratigraphers also analyze data from geophysical surveys that show the locations of stratigraphic units in the subsurface. Geophysical data and well logs can be combined to produce a better view of the subsurface, and stratigraphers often use computer programs to do this in three dimensions. In all cases, stratigraphers make interpretations of what they see and use those interpretations to construct a map of the geologic formations in the subsurface.
A standard geological or geological engineering report will begin with a written or graphic description or interpretation of the geologic and or geophysical data, a description and/or interpretation of the stratigraphic horizons and their boundaries, and finally an interpretation of the subsurface geologic features that the survey or drilling operations have encountered. The most accurate models are generally produced by combining field data (i.e., well log and core data, seismic data, geophysical data, etc.) with the data derived from laboratory and/or numerical analyses of the data. The interpretation or prediction of subsurface properties of a reservoir are commonly based on a mathematical simulation of the hydro-mechanics of the subsurface formation. For example, data from well logs (e.g., electrical, acoustic, nuclear and lithostatic) are typically combined with a numerical model to constrain the size and shape of the productive reservoir in a three-dimensional (3D) model. The most accurate numerical models of reservoir hydro-mechanics are those which take into account the presence of fractures and permeability anisotropy. Barred by the government from settling in New France, Huguenots led by Jessé de Forest, sailed to North America in 1624 and settled instead in the Dutch colony of New Netherland (later incorporated into New York and New Jersey); as well as Great Britain's colonies, including Nova Scotia. A number of New Amsterdam's families were of Huguenot origin, often having emigrated as refugees to the Netherlands in the previous century. In 1628 the Huguenots established a congregation as L'Église française à la Nouvelle-Amsterdam (the French church in New Amsterdam). Members of this congregation included Isaac de Pinto and Isaac de Pintra. They also sent representatives as delegates to the Synod of Dort in the Netherlands in 1618–41. Today, the Huguenots in New York have a sizable presence in the areas of education and finance.

There is a long history of tension between the Dutch and French colonies in New Amsterdam, which contributed to the eventual formation of the French and Dutch United Colonies in the seventeenth century. The tensions often broke out into conflict. During the seventeenth century, many of the settlers in the Dutch colony, mostly Dutch Catholics, were seeking religious freedom and tolerance under the Dutch Protestant government. They were sometimes persecuted by a new regime in Amsterdam for their beliefs. There were many conflicts and some deaths during the 17th century; the French settlers in the northern part of New Amsterdam, New France, were expelled from their homes in March 1665 following the fall of Quebec and New Netherlands to the English after the Siege of New Amsterdam in 1673 led by William Penn.

As is typical of the eighteenth-century diaspora of French Protestants, a few Huguenots settled in Pennsylvania and Delaware, while other Huguenot descendants of Louis XIV stayed in North America.

Under the Scotland Act 1998, ordinary general elections for the Scottish Parliament are held on the first Thursday in May every four years (1999, 2003, 2007 and so on). The date of the poll may be varied by up to one month either way by the Monarch on the proposal of the Presiding Officer.

The Scottish Parliament is not subject to the normal requirement of five-week campaigns, and instead normally campaigns from the day prior to the election to the day of the poll, and campaigns from the day prior to the poll to the day after.

In contrast, the UK Prime Minister normally campaigns for a Conservative or Labour candidate when contesting an English constituency or parliamentary seat - the latter is possible due to the special provision for Welsh and Scottish MPs. The day prior to the poll may be used as part of the campaign, as well as the time after the poll, but it is important to remain within the five-week polling period for the candidate to avoid disqualification as a result of the Electoral Commission.

If neither candidate secure a majority of the votes, the party with the most votes in their favour becomes the governing party in the newly elected Scottish Parliament, with the second place being allocated to the party with the second highest total number of votes, with a party who receives less votes being allocated the third place. This is known as 'proportional representation', where each voter elects one MP.

The Scottish Parliament has the same voting law as the rest of the United Kingdom. In the event of a tie, an individual vote is chosen by lot if any party or constituency has been eliminated and there is no candidate to which a majority has been given.

In contrast to Westminster elections, there is no 'first past the post' system for electing members. Instead, the individual votes elect one out of 73 members of the Parliament. Each candidate has the same number of votes, regardless of their party affiliation.

Baran developed the concept of distributed adaptive message block switching during his research at the RAND Corporation for the US Air Force into survivable communications networks, first presented to the Air Force in the summer of 1961 as briefing B-265, later published as RAND report P-2626 in 1962, and finally in report RM 3420 in 1964. Report P-2626 described a general architecture for a large-scale, distributed, survivable communications network. The concept of an adaptive message block switching layer that has distributed control and coordination in space and time, is at the heart of every aspect of Baran's research, including his paper on time-sharing networks,  time-sharing for networks: a study in distributed control and coordination,  and his 1963 paper Adaptive switching in two dimensions.

In the summer of 1961, he developed these concepts in work on the U.S. Air Force Project RAND in connection with their requirement of reliable, survivable, message switching. The result of this work was the publication of his paper Adaptive Message Block Switching in October 1961. (U.S.Air Force Project Report 6-20, July 1961)

Baran received the 1973 Turing Award from the Association for Computing Machinery "for his seminal contributions to the fundamental areas of computing theory and methodology and the development of the concept of distributed adaptive computer communication." Some theories developed in the 1970s established possible avenues through which inequality may have a positive effect on economic development. These have been largely explored in the context of the global South and are mostly focused on poverty. The basic idea of development being linked to the welfare of the poor has led some to theorise that poverty can be reduced as equality is enhanced. This is referred to as the poverty-efficiency link.

Other authors have suggested a reverse causal link, where inequality leads to poverty, with the poor becoming marginalised and excluded from the formal economy, as in the economic theory of class. This relationship is referred to as the inequality–poverty link. The latter view is often associated with Karl Polanyi. There is a theoretical debate on whether either of these links is likely to be relevant in China's development.

In China, inequality has increased sharply over the past two decades. In 2013, the country's per capita income was $6,600, still ranking among the bottom 10% in the world (see Poverty line on this page), albeit at a slightly higher level than in the 1990s. In the U.S. federal health care system (including the VA, the Indian Health Service, and NIH) ambulatory care pharmacists are given full independent prescribing authority. This means that pharmacists are allowed to prescribe drugs that they have identified, at doses and frequencies they decide, as medically appropriate based on the evidence that they gather during the process of evaluating an individual patient\'s particular situation. Such pharmacists may or may not have had some medical training in the past, but, in practice, they generally have received some training in pharmacology and are required to follow up with a patient and report adverse drug events (ADEs) that occur as a result of their independent use the American College of Clinical Pharmacy definition of medically appropriate drug therapy ([@bb0045]). In many, if not all, states pharmacists are also allowed to diagnose and treat patients. In the U.S., pharmacists are also allowed to prescribe drugs for off-label uses (unapproved by the U.S. Food and Drug Adminstration for use in humans) and for purposes of clinical research in the interest of improving patient care ([@bb0095]).

In the Australian health care system, pharmacists generally have only limited prescribing authority, with the majority being delegated the right to order only very simple and inexpensive generic generics (where they have been approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration; TGA), or those drugs that have a clear evidence base for their use in certain disease states and have been made available over the counter. text: Why has Japan's economy, once the envy of the world, fallen on such hard times, and why has recovery taken so long? The nine scholars analyzing Japan's economic crisis from 1985 through 2000 have identified six underlying causes:Surplus in Savings: Japan has traditionally enjoyed an unusually high savings rate and a comparatively low consumption rate. During the decades of recovery and high-speed growth, this "savings surplus" supplied sorely needed capital to private industry in the form of bank loans. Now private consumption, which accounts for two-thirds of the national economy, remains at Depression levels. Japan must now find new sources of industrial investment to sustain its economy.Favorable Saving Rates: One explanation for this "savings surplus" is the absence of a negative saving rate, or an interest rate that falls below the growth rate of the economy. The government's monetary targets for inflation and the exchange rate do not encourage this level of saving, which the economy needs to build up its capital base.Low Public and Market Investment: When private consumption fails to grow, governments must spend on infrastructure and social services to maintain living standards. The public sector accounts for roughly half of the national economy. Until 1993, Japan had a budget surplus, which meant that governments could finance large infrastructural investments from savings that were generated by lower public and market spending (the private sector's share of government spending is actually about one-third, according to economists). After 1993, government surpluses vanished and were never replaced with a surplus in private spending. The Rankine cycle is the fundamental thermodynamic underpinning of the steam engine. In its simplest form, a Rankine heat engine is composed of a boiler and a condenser ([Fig. 1](#F1){ref-type="fig"}). It uses the energy of a working fluid to drive a piston and converts it into an external rotary energy, which can then be transferred to a mechanical device that delivers work.

![Basic Rankine cycle for a single-cylinder engine.\
At a pressure lower than the vapor pressure, the working fluid will undergo steam expansion and undergo a phase change. The phase changes in the turbine generate additional pressure. Both the expansion and reduction in pressure cause the working fluid to evaporate into steam. In the cooling loop, the steam cools the working fluid using the latent heat of evaporation. The working fluid condenses and absorbs heat for phase change. The working fluid exits the condenser as a superheated vapor at a higher pressure than the boiler. Additional pressure is required to return the working fluid to the state where it can undergo another cycle of evaporation and expansion. In 2009, further fossils were found at the site, extending further back in time into the early Cambrian. The fossil is similar to the previous species, indicating that ctenophores changed very little throughout Cambrian time.

Ecology and physiology

Ctenophores have long been considered the most primitive extant animals. Ctenophores are bilaterally symmetric, have a radial symmetry of organization, are aplacophorans (comb-like bodies), and lack a defined nervous system. Within the genitourinary and gastrointestinal tracts, commensal flora serve as biological barriers by competing with pathogenic bacteria for food and space and, in some cases, by changing the conditions in their environment, such as pH or available iron. Commensal flora are therefore the first line of defense against pathogens in the gastrointestinal tract, as well as the first responders and regulators of host immune responses by producing antimicrobial compounds and soluble effector molecules, and as regulators of adaptive immune responses through production of cytokines and mucus. Bacteriocins are small antimicrobial peptides that are produced as ribosomally synthesized and posttranslationally modified molecules. They have various names, ranging from pyocins to microcins, depending on the type of organism from which they are isolated. Ctenophores are sometimes confused with jellyfish because they share a similar appearance and often inhabit the same areas. However, they are very different in appearance and, unlike cnidarian jellyfish, they cannot sting with a venom sac—rather, they possess ciliary bands that can entangle their prey. Sure, I had heard that generators in python and javascript could make certain things much nicer, but how often does one really need to have what appears to be nothing more than a fancy iterator? It wasn't until I followed this Rust RFC thread that the true potential of generators in Rust started to dawn on me.

The core idea of generators is to allow functions to yield data to clients, and then resume later once the clients request more data. Rust has an excellent iterator type called 'IterResult', and it's really quite easy to implement resumable versions of common functions like map. What I find surprising however, is how easy it is to introduce them to the world of Rust.

The problem with regular iterators and sequences is that they aren't composable, and are therefore not reusable in a way that is common in the world of functional programming and async programming. One of these teams discovered the plague bacterium in human faeces, at Tsan Yung Ling, a village near the border of China and Indochina, and in fleas in the village.

A century later, studies of DNA recovered from human teeth revealed that the plague bacterium from Tsan Yung ling belonged to the same group of bacteria as those responsible for the epidemic in modern Hong Kong. This finding indicates that the plague bacterium in Tsan Yung Ling may have been extinct for a few centuries, and it was probably reintroduced into the region sometime after Hong Kong’s colonial history. There have been relatively few cases of the plague throughout human history, and Tsan Yung Ling is probably the only place where the human pathogen was active for a long time. Victoria has a written constitution enacted in 1975, but based on the 1855 colonial constitution, passed by the United Kingdom Parliament as the Victoria Constitution Act 1855, which establishes the Parliament as the state's law-making body for matters coming under state responsibility. The executive is formally headed by a monarch, and a minister leads the executive branch, usually referred to as the Morrison ministry, named after the first non-Conservative PM. The head of the Legislative Assembly or lower house is known as the Speaker, and the head of the upper house National Capital Regional Council (NCR) is known as the President. The Governor General is an appointed ceremonial position and de facto the de jure head of state. Victoria has a bicameral system—the Legislature possesses both the authority to create laws with the power to amend or repeal them, and the authority to debate and discuss matters before they are passed or presented to the Executive.

The state's legislative power is reserved to the Parliament, whose members are chosen through a single vote. Legislative power is divided between the upper house Legislative Assembly, composed of the Legislative Assembly (full-time lower house) members and members of the National Capital Regional Council (NCR) (full-time upper house), and the Legislative Council (half-time upper house), elected from different geographical electorates (seats) in proportion to how their population is spread across the state. Both the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council can amend or repeal any legislation the Parliament passes, but not create new laws. The Constitution establishes the Legislative Council as a more powerful body than the Legislative Assembly and it has been used to protect Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the face of state discrimination and legislation that is not consistent with the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community's rights.

Most of the Rhine's current course was not under the ice during the last Ice Age; although, its source must still have been a glacier. A tundra, with Ice Age flora and fauna, stretched across middle Europe, from Asia to the Atlantic Ocean. Such was the case during the Last Glacial Maximum, ca. 20,000 to 15,000 years BP. Geographers refer to the northernmost extent of the tundra as the Weichselian glaciation, after a location in present-day Russia and Poland

It was not the only glacial event to take place throughout the Ice Age; there were also the Löwenstein (last interglacial phase), Eemian, and Devensian glaciations.

During the Löwenstein and Eemian glaciations, there were significant climate changes – some ice age glaciers were receding in Europe, and other areas where ice had been stable were now experiencing increased seasonal ice extent. This led to the onset of the Devensian glaciation, where the climate became extremely unstable. At the end of the Löwenstein, there was a transition, with the onset of a new glacial phase. Glaciers expanded into the tundra, and sea ice forms over the entire North Atlantic. This new glacial period was called the Riss glaciation.

The Riss phase is also called the Devensian Glaciation. The Riss glaciers began to retreat within 10,000 years, and by the year 9000, there was global warming for the first time during the entire Ice Age, which led to the disappearance of the glaciers. Most of today's rivers were formed during the Devensian glaciation.

Proportionality is recognised one of the general principles of European Union law by the European Court of Justice since the 1950s. According to the general principle of proportionality the lawfulness of an action depends on whether it was appropriate and necessary to achieve the objectives legitimately pursued. As has been stated by the Court: "the purpose of the principle is to ensure that the law is based on reason and that it is proportionate. It requires every Act of a legislative nature to reconcile, where possible, the freedom of the legal person with the requirements of justice and the general good, and the protection and respect for the rights of an individual, with the needs of public life and society." As observed by C v Commission [1991] ECR I-4710, the principle of proportionality has been applied on two levels, to the substance and the form of the laws. In the first instance the proportionality test is applicable to each particular measure. The Court states in that judgment: "The concept of proportionality, as used in art 2(1) of the Treaty and applied in this judgment, may be interpreted broadly as referring to the legal aspects relating to (i) the justification of the existence, character, duration and content of the measures and (ii) the relationship between the objective pursued by the measures and their means employed. The principle is not confined to the existence of justifications which are formally recognised as reasons for adopting the measure, be it in its content, its duration and its content or its application".

In his judgment, Lord Carswell states that "the principle of proportionality is an essential ingredient in any system of law. We’re all living longer, and ageing is a part of life and not a disease

European Union law is a body of treaties and legislation, such as Regulations and Directives, which have direct effect or indirect effect on the laws of European Union member states. Directives, Regulations, etc. enter into domestic legal force only when they are adopted in the form of Community instruments (EC treaties) by way of the Council of Ministers. As Community instruments, Directives then enter into force for both EU citizens and residents of an EU state, but Regulations do not. EU legal instruments may be of "direct effect" (in that they give a direct effect to a treaty) or "indirect effect" (in that they give an indirect effect to a previous treaty). As such, the law of the European Union is "the first pillar" or "the second pillar" of the single legal sphere envisaged and sought through the creation of the European Union, and it should be harmonised.

The European Union's founding treaties

The treaties which created the European Union were the Basic Treaty, the Treaty of Rome and the Treaty of Amsterdam.

The Basic Treaty

The Basic Treaty for the European Union was adopted by the representatives of the European political class in Helsinki, Finland on the 21st December 1977. It entered into force in June of the following year, although no amendments were tabled in subsequent years. This treaty created the European Community from the six existing member states of Euroland, and it would later be extended to the rest of the continent by the Treaty of Amsterdam (and subsequently by the Treaty of Nice). The Basic Treaty also established the Union's executive apparatus, the European Commission and the European Parliament.

The Treaty of Rome

The Treaty of Rome entered into force on April 1st 1958, replacing the Basic Treaty as the supreme legal document of the Community

Robert Altman's downbeat, new-fangled western from Edmund Naughton's book ""McCabe"" was overlooked at the time of its release but in the past years has garnered a sterling critical following. Aside from a completely convincing boom-town scenario, the characters here don't merit much interest, and the picture looks (intentionally) brackish and unappealing. Bearded Warren Beatty plays a turn-of-the-century entrepreneur who settles in struggling community on the outskirts of nowhere and helps organize the first brothel; once the profits start coming in, Beatty is naturally menaced by city toughs who want part of the action.

While Beatty is, of course, a fine actor, it's impossible to imagine the film's mawkishness taking anyone's heart. For the sake of clarity, let's make one thing clear: what this film doesn't contain is violence nor even blood. It's a slow, deliberately unappealing movie directed by Altman in a deliberate, unappealing way: the slow-motion scenes, shot in tight close-ups, show the actors' faces floating off the camera like bubbles, and everything moves in a languid circle. Altman, himself, plays a character called "Mr. McCabe," whose job is simply to be there, sitting around, watching. What there is of plot, in terms of a struggle between man and circumstances, involves four members of a family (Mr. McCabe, his wife Sylvia, their son and his fiance), and it's never really made clear why each is so enmeshed in the situation they're mired in. After a while, even the audience loses interest in who's winning out of all this, until the end, when everything seems to fall in place.

Altman's best work, after, has to be "Nashville, " which featured a terrific performance by Beatty (in one of his first great films) as a man who falls in love with an actress without knowing who she really is. "McCabe" is pretty good, but the one for me would be the final scene in "M*A*S*

Because the problem P = NP is not solved, being able to reduce a known NP-complete problem, Π2, to another problem, Π1, would indicate that there is no known polynomial-time solution for Π1. This is because a polynomial-time solution to Π1 would yield a polynomial-time solution to Π2.

Polynomial-time solutions

A problem Π has a polynomial-time solution if there is a polynomial-time algorithm A for finding a solution to Π, and there is no polynomial-time algorithm B to decide Π for all instances, but there are some problems A1,..., An where Π = A1,..., An. We say that A is a polynomial-time solution for Π. The complexity of a polynomial-time solution depends on the complexity of the algorithm for finding solutions. This is because finding solutions to Π is just as hard as solving (determining if Π is true or false) for all Πs. For instance, the first polynomial-time hierarchy theorem describes how to "simulate" Π by enumerating all partial solutions.

Uniflow engines attempt to remedy the difficulties arising from the usual counterflow cycle where, during each stroke, the port and the cylinder walls will be cooled by the passing exhaust steam, whilst the hotter incoming admission steam will waste some of its energy in restoring working temperature. This may reduce the volumetric efficiency of the engines.
For the purposes of avoiding this, the basic concept of a uniflow engine is to use the hot exhaust gases as driving medium for a pump that displaces the admission steam from the inlets to the cylinder to the exhaust outlets. The engine itself produces no useful power (except to drive the pump), so to get a useful amount of work out of the heat of the exhaust there must be some way of redirecting waste heat into the surrounding environment. In order to transfer all of the heat that would normally dissipate into the exhaust gases into something useful, a heat sink is required. Traditionally this is a heat exchanger, as in a conventional steam engine, and in order to make it a heat sink, one of the fluids, usually the exhaust steam, must be at a low temperature. A uniflow engine has a hot part that must be cooled. This is made possible by the fact that the uniflow heat sink must be in a closed loop and the volume of the engine must be significantly larger than that of a usual single heat exchanger with exhaust steam, and this is exactly the situation required for an air to engine heat exchange. mucormycosis is a rare infection caused by the ubiquitous filamentous fungi of the order mucorales and class zygomycetes . these species are vasotropic , causing rapid onset of tissue infarctions and necrosis and subsequent thrombosis by invading vascular bed . the disease spectrum ranges from involvement of skin , sinuses , lung , and brain to disseminated and mostly fatal infections , especially in immunocompromised hosts . its clinical course is usually acute and is characterized by a progressive course, high mortality, and delayed diagnosis.[ 1 ]

The order mucorales are a group of opportunistic fungi and are among the most common pathogenic fungi found in nature. In contrast to aspergillus spp and other fungi, mucormycosis typically grows in clusters that contain asexual spores and have a dark "saucer-shaped" appearance that differs from the saprophytic varieties of the group. Mucorales inhabit soil and water and are ubiquitous and commonly found in environments that are characterized by warm, moist, and alkaline soils. Most species of the Order can be found in the oral cavity or in the gastrointestinal tract. This fact and their capacity to grow rapidly in areas that are poorly aerated increase the opportunity for exposure to hosts, particularly in poorly ventilated hospitals and other institutions where individuals are confined to a bed or a wheelchair. [ 2 ] The incidence of mucormycosis has steadily increased since the early 1990 s.[ 3, 4 ]

The infection most often presents as progressive thrombotic and necrotizing lesions in vascular districts like the skin, sinuses, kidneys and the lung. Although it can affect almost every organ system, the central nervous system is most commonly affected. Neurologic manifestations include headaches, vision loss, convulsions, seizures and coma, and a high mortality rate is reported in cases with a long-standing or invasive lesion. [ 2, 5 ]

Several barriers protect organisms from infection, including mechanical, chemical, and biological barriers. The skin serves as a significant physical barrier providing protection against pathogens. The outermost layer of the skin, the stratum corneum, consists of an extremely dense layer of dead cells. This dead layer is itself composed of corneocytes, which are flattened, keratinized cells. Despite its apparent impenetrability, transient aqueous holes in the corneum occur naturally as part of the process of desquamation. These natural aqueous channels have been exploited for a variety of applications including drug delivery, cosmetic applications, and other areas.
The stratum corneum is a complex structure, consisting of corneocytes, lipid bilayers, and intercellular structures. Stratum corneum lipids are organized in discrete domains, including keratin-enriched domains, ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids, and phospholipids. The intercellular elements consist of fibrillar structures including collagen fibrils and elastin microfibrils.
Despite its apparent impermeability, the stratum corneum is actually a very dynamic and responsive structure, and it has been shown that it is somewhat plastic. It can be penetrated by a large spectrum of molecules, including water, lipophilic molecules, and topical or systemic pharmacologic agents.
Intercellular lipids, such as ceramides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids prevent or retard the permeation of other molecules. A Turing machine is a mathematical model of a general computing machine. It is a theoretical device that manipulates symbols contained on a strip of tape. Turing machines are not intended as a practical computing technology, but rather as a thought experiment representing a computing machine—anything from an advanced supercomputer to a mathematician with a pencil and paper. To date, all of the work in formalizing them in a precise way has been done by researchers in the field of theoretical computer science, in particular on the basis of the Church–Turing thesis.

A theoretical device

When people speak about a "Turing machine" they usually mean a formal description of the Turing machine, a mathematical model used to describe computing machines. The formalization of Turing's ideas in a logical system dates from the 1940s. When the ideas about a machine that manipulates symbols on a strip of paper were presented, it was natural to think of the symbols, or the tape, or both as a series of squares. John von Neumann's idea of a linear sequence was to consider the symbols in a series of rows, one above the other, each row extending for n symbols, where n is the length of the strip of paper. After the row is filled it is marked "1" for all its values in an attempt to represent the machine's progress. This was von Neumann's (non-mathematical) first formalization of a computing machine. He never used the actual terminology "linear Turing machine". He preferred "Turing machine", because people who knew what he was talking about understood what that meant and some people who did not knew what he was talking about could be led to believe "Turing machine" was some kind of an animal. Almost all ctenophores are predators – there are no vegetarians and only one genus that is partly parasitic. If food is plentiful, they can eat 10 times their own weight per day. While Beroe preys mainly on other ctenophores, other surface-water species prey on zooplankton (planktonic animals) ranging in size from the microscopic, including mollusc and fish larvae, to small adult crustaceans such as copepods, amphipods, and even krill.

Most species of ctenophores are transparent, with a columnar body, and are not very colourful, but the larvae of several of the sea lilies (Doliolida), such as Halocrispedum capense and Lophogorgia gracilis, are beautifully coloured. Some of the ctenophores have a long, retractile tentacle protruding from the middle of the mouth. When fully extended, these tentacles will capture a prey animal and drag it against the surface in such a way that the prey becomes a part of the sea lily.

While sea lilies are filter-feeding animals, the other ctenophores – the comb-jellies (Merryfellsia) – are scavengers, although they are opportunist feeders. Ctenophores swim freely on the surface, but occasionally they can drop down into the depths (they cannot swim faster than their body shape allows) and stay there for a time (up to one week).

Sea lilies have short, simple and unjointed arms only half the length of the body. Most are carnivorous and are found almost everywhere, being widespread from the tropics to 60°N, and from the Atlantic to the Antarctic Ocean. Some species are found almost exclusively in fresh water.

Culturally, ctenophores are becoming increasingly important because of their ability to undergo parthenogenesis, a process whereby unfertilised female animals can produce offspring without mating. However, some ctenophores are sexually reproducing.

In Van Gend en Loos v Nederlandse Administratie der Belastingen it was held that the provisions of the Treaties (and EU Regulations) are directly effective, if they are (1) clear and unambiguous (2) unconditional, and (3) did not require EU or national authorities to take further action to implement them. Van Gend en Loos, a postal company, claimed that what is now TFEU article 30 prevented the Dutch Customs Authorities charging tariffs, when it imported urea-formaldehyde plastics from Germany to the Netherlands. The Dutch government resisted, on behalf of the Dutch Customs Authorities. The court unanimously agreed with the Dutch government. The court stated that "the intention of the legislator [who drafted the EU Treaty] was to give the EU citizen the opportunity to rely on direct effect in the areas of tax and VAT in those cases where he can claim that the application of an Act of the legislator in question will directly result in a direct, but not automatic, burden on him.". This test was later used by the Italian court in Alcoa-Gorda and Nave della Regina Coeli [2001] IT-II, in order "to check whether the law is a true and correct embodiment of the decision of the legislator or a mere draft in which the legislator's intention is not absolutely certain".

Van Gend en Loos and several other cases decided around the same time indicate that where an EU law is not directly effective, it may still have indirect effects, for instance if EU law allows the member State responsible to claim a right of access to the Court of Justice, that should not, according to Van Gend, hinder that member state to bring an action in its own courts instead. Such an indirect effect can also arise from EU law if, for example, it gives one of the parties a right of appeal to a court, and that party then chooses the court that will hear this case. A plate boundary, i.e. where two plates come in contact with one another, or subduct away from one another, in response to the spreading of the lithosphere, results in the development of a transform zone of asthenosphere. During this process the uppermost portion of the mantle is stretched and thinned. This stretching and thinning of the asthenosphere causes the transformation of the previously passive state of the asthenosphere, the asthenodynamo, into an active dynamo, the lithospheric dynamo. At the beginning of the 20th century, important advancement in geological science was facilitated by the ability to obtain accurate absolute dates to geologic events using radioactive isotopes and other methods. This changed the understanding of geologic time. Until this time, it was commonly believed that the Earth's stratigraphic history consisted of long, gradual and continuous changes called geologic periods.  Periods were subdivided into stages, and stages into more recent, epochs.  It was also assumed that the Earth's stratigraphic history was cyclic, and that the present strata were the same as the earliest existing stratigraphic formations.  Such an assumption was reasonable since it was not until the beginning of the 19th century that geologists were required to record the age of stratigraphic formations and events as accurate absolute dates using various types of radioactive dating methods.  By the early twentieth century, scientists determined that the Earth's strata were not the same, and that most strata could no longer be assumed to have existed for a given length of time. Geologists realized that the stratigraphic history of the Earth's surface changed drastically within small regions, or even from point to point on a region (this is known as the regional sequence method of geologists).

Almost all ctenophores are predators, taking prey ranging from microscopic larvae and rotifers to the adults of small crustaceans; the exceptions are juveniles of two species, which live as parasites on the salps on which adults of their species feed. In favorable circumstances, ctenophores can eat ten times their own weight in a day. Only 100–150 species have been validated, and possibly another 25 have not been fully described and named. A recent estimate by Glynn et al. puts the total number of ctenophore species at 1500. More than half of these have been described only in the last ten years. Despite the number of new valid species being high, in a review of the known ctenophores, Berglund & Bergström estimate that only five or six major lineages have evolved since they first appeared in the fossil record (about 1.5 billion years ago).

Ctenophores feed with a tentacle-like proboscis and with various muscular and usually sticky cilia, in such a manner that they have no definite digestive tract on their bodies. They have one of the few examples of holobiont, in which a phytoplankton parasite contains some tissues and organs of its host. Ctenophores are a group of organisms that are intermediate in some respects between single-cell algae and molluscs. The Black Death is thought to have originated in the arid plains of Central Asia, where it then travelled along the Silk Road, reaching Crimea by 1343. From there, it was most likely carried by Oriental rat fleas living on the black rats that were regular passengers on merchant ships. Spreading throughout the Mediterranean and Europe, the Black Death is estimated to have killed 30–60% of Europe's total population. The year 1348 is often referred to as the time when the Black Death was at its most deadly in Europe.

Contents show]

The Black Death was one of the most devastating periods in European history, with a population decline of a third. The Black Death has since entered the popular consciousness as the worst pandemic catastrophe of the Medieval Period, the first of the Three Plague Epidemic Periods to come, the first to appear since the Middle Ages, and the third-deadliest infectious disease outbreak in history. It is also the only recorded pandemic to start in Asia before spreading to Europe. The Black Death became the world's "first modern pandemic" after it spread to the Middle East and North Africa, and continues to exist today, appearing periodically in various forms, including the bubonic plague[2] and smallpox.

There is little consensus among historians regarding the causes of the Black Death[3][4][5][6][7][8] and estimates of its mortality vary between 20% and 100%.[9] While there is evidence of the presence of bubonic plague bacteria, the exact origin of the epidemic remains unknown. Closely related fields in theoretical computer science are analysis of algorithms and computability theory.

Algorithms
Algorithms are mathematical procedures that can be performed by a computer to solve a (computer-understood) problem. The main goal of an algorithm is to solve a problem with a specific level of precision and with as few steps as possible. By comparison, mathematical proofs solve problems "cleanly" in the sense that they require extremely few steps, but without any need to define, measure or quantify how much time it takes to solve a problem or what a specific step means in time or space.

Most problems are computationally intractable, meaning that solving them (in the sense of polynomial time) is at least as hard (if not more so) than solving many other problems. However, some problems can be solved efficiently by a computer. Many efficient algorithms can be found in the fields of complexity theory, cryptography, and computer science.

An NP-complete problem is one whose solution cannot be decided in polynomial time without employing exponential resources. Many problems from artificial intelligence and natural language processing are NP-complete according to the theory of NP-completeness developed by Richard Karp, Leonid Levin, and Stephen Cook over the 1960s and early 1970s. NP-complete problems also often have efficient algorithms for some restricted cases. For example, the traveling salesman problem can be solved with an exponential-time (polynomial-time) algorithm, but most problems in the theory of computational complexity require only polynomial-time algorithms.

Some civil disobedience defendants choose to make a defiant speech, or a speech explaining their actions, in allocution. In U.S. v. Burgos-Andujar, a defendant who was involved in a movement to stop military exercises by trespassing on U.S. Navy property argued to the court in allocution that "the ones who are violating the greater law are the members of the Navy". As a result, the judge increased her sentence from 40 to 60 days.

In U.S. v. L'Enfant, a defendant who entered the territory of the government of the Republic of the Philippines, which was an object of illegal occupation by the U.S., argued in his allocution to the court that one of the principles of international law was that "no person can be treated like a colonial subject". As a result, his sentence was increased from 2 years and 6 months to 1 year and 8 months.

Some individuals and groups claim that they may choose to plead guilty, but that they should be allowed to explain their motivations and their arguments for guilt. The courts have refused this plea under the premise that it is inadmissible self-incrimination, but more recently there is a trend to have allocutions by the accused. An example is the decision of the Supreme Court of Australia, which held that an allocution to the facts by the accused on their sentence for their crime is always permitted when the prosecution is demanding a sentence of at least three years. The only restriction is if the accused confesses to an unrelated crime.

Since the late 20th century, when the practice of allowing allocutions came out, this has become a common practice in cases involving defendants accused of violent crimes, whether sexual or otherwise. In the case of R v. Smith in 2010, the defendant plead guilty to the crime of "assault with a weapon or attempt to cause bodily harm" on a police officer. The court accepted the allocution with the understanding that it was a plea for an apology and a lenient sentence.

The concept of duty was first introduced by Watt in order to illustrate how much more efficient his engines were over the earlier Newcomen designs. Duty is the number of foot-pounds of work delivered by burning one bushel (94 pounds) of coal. Thus Watt's engines delivered at least 8 times more work with one pound of coal than his predecessor's engines; this is also true for all steam engines operating at high altitudes and is generally known as the “8 x” rule.
Since the 1880's, the standard units of measurement of work in the UK and USA have been  and, respectively. With these units, the average Watt's engine had a duty of at least 0.64.

An engine with a higher duty factor delivered a greater amount of work for the same weight of fuel. This is because a higher duty factor gives the engine many more cycles per bushel of coal and the power stroke of the piston makes the greatest mechanical advantage per cycle.

Comparisons 
Because higher duty requires more coal to be used, a more powerful steam engine will tend to burn more fuel. In a steam engine with a fixed heat transfer surface area, a higher duty would allow the amount of steam to rise to a level where it is needed for the process. Tentulae and tentilla are generally not present in adult or larval stages. Adult ctenophores attach themselves by one or more short mucus threads, or monilia, from the oral surface to the walls of the coelenteron, the internal cavity housing the body cavity. The monilia may be in the form of a flat moniliform ribbon, but more typically form a loose or dense cluster, called a lophophore. This cluster is usually divided across the oral/aboral axis, the two divisions bearing on or near opposite poles of the body. During attachment to the substrate, usually a scleropodium of subumbrellar cilia is often erected. An additional, rarely occurring form is the moniliform ribbon lying perpendicular to the side.

to perform tasks , organisms often use multiple procedures . For example, suppose a monkey digs the dirt for a new home, cleans the burrow of excrement, and then makes certain that the burrow is completely secure. The monkey may use multiple strategies and different activities to secure a burrow. However, all of the activities are done to ensure the burrow is well-protected. For another example, consider that of a mother and child in which the mother performs multiple activities simultaneously to protect her child. In both cases (digging a new burrow and child protection) there are multiple activities that are often carried out simultaneously. We will refer to these activities in Chapter 4 as _motor behaviors,_ which include tasks such as digging, eating, drinking, grooming, and caring for offspring (N. L. Brown [2011] 2011). The goal of motor behavior is to ensure that all of these tasks are performed. That is, motor behaviors often occur simultaneously and are not performed in a single, sequential series.

What Does It Mean to Do Multiple Activities Simultaneously?

Motor behaviors can be thought of as actions that are organized by the nervous system in a given order to complete a given task. If a particular action such as digging is complete, then that does not mean that the subject has performed all of the behaviors necessary to do that activity. Steam-driven turbines are commonly used for power conversion in open loop Rankine cycle operations, primarily because they generate high levels of power for a given weight of system. There are other advantages as well including the ability to easily adjust the system to increase or decrease power output, and the ability to quickly "warm-up" the power generating equipment. Typically exhaust steam from the turbine is condensed by direct contact with cooled ambient air.
Steam-driven turbines have been widely used in industrial systems for many years. They are often the most energy efficient solution for power conversion. This efficiency, or ratio between the mechanical power available to the turbine impeller for each unit of water converted, is commonly referred to as Coefficient of Performance (COP). They are called fuzzy observables, because, in general, they don’t commute with quantum observables. An example of a decision problem is the following. The input is an arbitrary graph. The problem consists in deciding whether the given graph is connected, or not.

If we take two arbitrary vertices v and w of an arbitrary graph G, then there exist a pair of edges e=(v,w) and e'=(w,v), such that the graph obtained from G deleting the edges e and e' is connected.

In other words, the problem to be solved consists in deciding whether there exists a partition V=A∪B of the vertex set V(G) of the graph such that the graph obtained by deleting the vertices v and e' with the pair of edges that form the partition A∪B is connected, or not.

This problem cannot exist, since it would be possible to determine whether the graph G was connected, by looking at any vertex v of the graph.

To solve this problem, we cannot take e and the vertex w, because if we take v, e, and w would be a subset of the vertex v, but that would be impossible.

Instead, one can take e'=(u,v); the fact that the graph obtained by deleting e' and e is connected means that, if we take v, e, and e', then u and v are not adjacent, so the fact that e' and e are adjacent implies that u and e' are not adjacent, and hence u and v are not adjacent either.

So, to find a vertex v such that we can prove that v is not connected in v to anything, we need to find that one vertex v whose deletion ensures the connectivity of G.

This problem is defined at the level of individual graphs, not at the level of classes of graphs.

The Rhine was not known to Herodotus and first enters the historical period in the 1st century BC in Roman-era geography. At that time, it formed the boundary between Gaul and Germania.

The Romans constructed their most important military supply centre of the Gallic territory at Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, or Cologne, (modern-day Koeln), at the confluence of the Rhine and the Lippe. The city, built in the 1st century BC and continuously inhabited until AD 1442, gradually declined following the collapse of the Western Roman Empire, after which control of the river valley passed to a successor state like the Franks. By the start of the 5th century the river had been incorporated within their own kingdoms, and the Franks also controlled its mouth. The Franks, under the leadership of the Merovingian dynasty and under the sway of the Carolingian dynasty of the Frankish Empire, held that control until the 15th century when it was annexed by the Holy Roman Empire: thereafter it became the western frontier of the Empire. This region and the river and its tributaries formed one of the major riverine highways for traders in northern Europe, as the Rhine marks the boundary between the areas that had been directly ruled by the Roman Empire—the Germanic kingdoms north of it—and the regions to the west that were part of the Visigothic kingdom, the Roman province of Britannia, or the Saxon kingdoms to the south. These kingdoms became the historical roots of modern-day France, Germany, and the UK.

When rock units are placed under horizontal compression, they shorten and become thicker. Because rock units, other than muds, do not significantly change in volume, this is accomplished in two primary ways: through faulting and folding. In the shallow crust, where brittle deformation can occur, thrust faults form, which cause deeper rock to move on top of shallower rock. The thrust can extend across a formation for miles, and then fold and dip to the next formation. Folds can form from horizontal extension and contraction of a formation, typically in response to an overlying mass of rock pressing down on it. This may also cause movement of a formation relative to its host.

Background:The incidence of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuritis (NAION) varies substantially among different countries. The aim of our study was to investigate its distribution in Japan. Materials and methods:We analyzed data collected in Japan between 2005 and 2013. Incidence, gender and age differences, the seasonal variation of NAION cases, the year-to-year variation of NAION rates, and the age-specific prevalence rates were compared between the years 2005–2011 and 2012–2013. Results: The yearly incidence of NAION was relatively stable in Japan during 2005–2013. More men were affected than women. The yearly incidence peaked in the age range of 40–49 years. There was a strong seasonal variation in the onset of NAION. Incidence rates for the spring-summer season were higher and for the autumn-winter season were lower than those for the other seasons. The incidence increased from 2009 to 2013. The prevalence rate was highest among persons aged 60–69 years, followed by 30–39-year and 70–79-year-olds. Conclusions: The incidence of NAION in Japan appears to be stable. However, the trend towards earlier onset may be emerging.

The success of any pathogen depends on its ability to elude host immune responses. Therefore, pathogens evolved several methods that allow them to successfully infect a host, while evading detection or destruction by the immune system. Bacteria often overcome physical barriers by secreting enzymes that digest the barrier, for example, by using a type II secretion system.

Many type II secretion systems have evolved to penetrate the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. Ranging from about 1 millimeter (0.039 in) to 1.5 meters (4.9 ft) in size, ctenophores are the largest non-colonial animals that use cilia ("hairs") as their main method of locomotion. Most species have eight strips, called comb rows, that run the length of their bodies and bear comb-like bands of cilia, called "ctenes," stacked along the comb rows so that when the cilia beat, those of each comb touch the comb below. Ctenophores are closely related to jellyfish, but do not have any stinging cells or venom.

Ctenophores are known for being exceptionally cryptic creatures, but they are still extremely well-known for their wide variety of color patterns, unusual behavior, and unique appearance.

The most well-known ctenophore of all is the comb jelly, Ctenophora, which can have a striking blue, red, or yellow coloration. This is primarily done through symbiotic associations with bioluminescent bacteria, which form glowing patterns that outline the ctene bands. Blue comb jellies form deep-sea communities of hundreds to thousands of specimens that drift with ocean currents, while red and yellow comb jellies reside in shallow and intermediate water levels, and sometimes float in the wake of fish like tuna. Ctenophores generally have a round body and an elongated funnel-shaped trunk, in which the comb rows are located. All ctenophores have a single mouth, but ctene rows tend to run most of the body length and form long, thin tentacles at the termini of the ctene rows, which cover the animal's body at all times except when using its tentacles to capture prey.

Most Ctenophora are filter-feeders like the jellyfish

Largely forgettable tale in which mercenary Kerman & employer Agren travel into the jungle in search of Agren's missing sister.

Despite its connection to the cannibal movie family, this film is more of an extreme version of Rene Cardona's ""Guyana - Crime of the Century"". Lenzi clearly aims to exploit the (at that time) topical Jonestown massacre, by depicting a rogue, self righteous zealot with a penchant for bigamy and just a hint of megalomania (played with ruthless intensity by Ivan Rassimov) leading his motley crew flock into self inflicted oblivion. With sister in toe, Kerman & Agren attempt to stop the rot, but after several failed coups, they end up fleeing into the ""Green Inferno"", only to run afoul the locals and their notorious appetites.

One in a string of excessive gore fests that emerged in the late seventies/early eighties, where every new addition seemed to engage in a one-upmanship contest with its predecessor, by attempting to contrive the most gory and graphic display ever brought to motion pictures. And it's safe to say that it all comes down to a contest with, ""Soylent Green is People"", where the only thing more extreme, is that in this case the "people" are cannibals!

The story, a variation on the infamous ""Bloody Meadows Massacre"", also involves other cannibalistic cults who had ties to Jonestown. One of these groups, led by Agren's sister, was led by a certain Jim Jones (John Phillip Law), in what many (including him) took as an act of vengeance for a previous disagreement. This all proves to be an unfortunate mistake, with the locals who had no prior knowledge, promptly running the misguided cult members through with machetes and hacking off their limbs. The film is filled with various graphic images that are far too graphic for a PG film; with much of the human gore seen in a rather voyeuristic manner, as if the local natives were actually enjoying seeing the savages (especially Jim Jones himself) being slaughtered. While the director's intention may have been to create a rather graphic piece of cinema, it's obvious that had the film been made later, with the PG rating in place, it could have been just as good (although I imagine more likely terrible) without the bloodbath and gore!

diffusion studies of adsorbates moving on a surface are often analyzed using 2d langevin simulations . The use of a full time-dependent diffusion model would make it possible to study the effect of substrate and electrode geometry on the steady state as well as transient behavior of adsorbates on surfaces. In the 2d langevin, the electrode potential can be modeled differently from the 3d langevin; the 2d langevin cannot distinguish between the two electrodes, whereas the 3d langevin can and does account for it. It is possible that differences between these models arise in the steady state behavior of these surface reactions. We have therefore conducted 2d langevin simulations of surface diffusion on the Pd(100) and (111) surfaces. We find that the 2d langevin model can be used to study the adsorption of H$_2$ on both of these surfaces.

In the case of an infinite Pd(111) surface, we see that the 2d langevin model gives more accurate estimates of H$_2$ partial pressures than the 3d langevin model does. Furthermore, we find the 2d langevin model predicts that the steady state partial pressure is independent of substrate voltage and that the 2d langevin is more accurate than the 3d langevin for predicting the full relaxation state. In the case of the Pd(100) surface, we find that the predictions of the 2d langevin model are qualitatively better. The 3d langevin model predicts that the steady state partial pressure is independent of substrate voltage. Both models can be used to study the evolution of the partial pressure into equilibrium and subsequent relaxation at the surfaces. Overall therefore, the 2d langevin model can be used to predict steady state behavior of these surface reactions whereas the 3d langevin model cannot.

Pathogens can rapidly evolve and adapt, and thereby avoid detection and neutralization by the immune system; however, multiple defense mechanisms have also evolved to recognize and neutralize pathogens. Even simple unicellular organisms such as bacteria possess a rudimentary immune system, in the form of enzymes that protect against bacteriophage infections. Other basic immune mechanisms evolved in ancient eukaryotes and remain in their modern descendants, such as plants and invertebrates. Innate immunity and adaptive immunity, two major branches of immunity in animals, are also evolutionarily ancient. Among the more specialized examples of antimicrobial protection are immune and non-immune antibodies, as well as various complement molecules and other effector molecules. These mechanisms differ by the manner in which they recognize and neutralize pathogens, but they all work by causing damage to the target. Therefore, although pathogens evolve mechanisms to disrupt or avoid these damaging actions, they ultimately must face the reality of killing by immune or non-immune effectors.

Another high-profile example of affirmative action came when the University of Texas announced in May that it would require women to have a grade point average (GPA) of 3.40 out of four during the final two semesters of their undergraduate careers to keep their degrees. This was despite the fact that a grade of “B” or “B +” was sufficient for graduation with minimal work experience at many employers. DECnet is a suite of network protocols created by Digital Equipment Corporation, originally released in 1975 in order to connect two PDP-11 minicomputers. It evolved into one of the first peer-to-peer network architectures, thus transforming DEC into a networking powerhouse in the 1980s. DECnet is optimized for the needs of batch (job control) and distributed computing environments, rather than for the needs of individual desktop users.

In the first half of the 17th century, a plague claimed some 1.7 million victims in Italy, or about 14% of the population. In 1656, the plague killed about half of Naples' 300,000 inhabitants. The plague was also a major cause of mortality across Europe. In Europe, mortality peaked at 15% in Amsterdam in 1654. It never surpassed 15% in England or France, although the proportion of deaths attributed to the disease varied greatly, from about 8% in London to about 50% in Marseilles, and even 80% in parts of the Spanish Levant. The epidemics in the Spanish Levant (in Syria, Palestine, and Lebanon) in 1713–1714 are considered the worst since the Black Death. Mortality rate may have reached as high as 30–50% percent in parts of Europe.

By the end of the seventeenth century, plague was already nearly eradicated from Europe (less than one reported case was recorded for the year 1708 in England), in most of Western Europe (but not in Portugal) during the 18th century.

In the second half of the 17th century, plague continued to occur and was still in many European settlements a major cause of mortality. A steam turbine consists of one or more rotors (rotating discs) mounted on a drive shaft, alternating with a series of stators (static discs) fixed to the turbine casing. The rotors have a propeller-like arrangement of blades at the outer edge. Steam acts upon these blades, producing rotary motion. The turbine casing, which contains the rotors within the space between the outer and inner surfaces of the casing, is fixed to the turbine casing by a suitable gasket. Water steam passing through the turbine in a closed space between the stationary casing and the inner surface of the rotor causes a pressure drop, and the working steam forces the blades of the rotors to rotate which in turn rotate the rotor shaft.
U.S. Pat. No. 4,073,322 (Lindahl) teaches that the efficiency of a steam turbine, as well as the maximum shaft speed of the turbine can be increased by providing a labyrinth sealing system in the space between the rotor and the stationary casing. Other sealing systems are well known in the steam turbine field. They include:
(a) Sealing of the low pressure side by providing a circumferential labyrinth of apertures and/or pins in the stators (static discs), surrounding at least one set of rotor blades;

While acknowledging the central role economic growth can potentially play in human development, poverty reduction and the achievement of the Millennium Development Goals, it is becoming widely understood amongst the development community that special efforts must be made to ensure poorer sections of society are able to participate in economic growth. The effect of economic growth on poverty reduction – the growth elasticity of poverty – can depend on the existing level of inequality. For instance, with low inequality a country with a growth rate of 2% per head and 40% of its population living in poverty, can halve poverty in ten years, but a country with high inequality would take nearly 60 years to achieve the same reduction. The effect therefore on poverty reduction if the Gini coefficient increased by 1%, will be quite different.

Econometric analysis of data from a comprehensive assessment of Latin America by UNDP (PEPAL 2006) indicates the following. Brazil has the highest growth elasticity of poverty, with the poorest part of society doubling their incomes between 2001 to 2005. Peru has a growth elasticity of poverty of 0.77 while Bolivia has one of 0.39. In Guatemala and Paraguay, the poorest quartile have experienced little change in their incomes between 2001 and 2005, with poverty decreasing between 0.05 and 0.07% points in both countries.

The effect of growth on income distribution is therefore very heterogeneous across Latin American countries and has a considerable dependence on initial inequality levels. A study by UNDP in 2004, also found large cross-country variations in the reduction in poverty in the region in the decade 2000 to 2010. With the growth in poverty between 2001 and 2005 falling slightly in most of the countries analyzed, Colombia, Ecuador, El Salvador and Honduras experienced the largest reductions in poverty, while Haiti, Dominican Republic, Jamaica and Panama experienced the poorest performance.

The effect of economic growth on poverty is also closely related to income inequality between countries. As the figure below indicates, in low inequality countries, like Brazil, Peru, Ecuador, Brazil and Mexico, the poverty head count has significantly decreased while in more unequal nations like Chile, Colombia, Haiti and Costa Rica, poverty has actually increased between 2001 and 2005. At all levels of inequality, income growth is very important to poverty reduction. However, a growth rate of less than 2% per head per year in the highest inequality countries can lead to the greatest deterioration in poverty.

interferon- ( ifn- )  is an essential cytokine for immunity against intracellular pathogens and cancer . It acts to confer protective immunity against viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites. The type I IFN is a small, structurally related proteins that binds to cell surface receptors called the ( ifn- ) receptor. It is secreted by virtually all cell types to mediate antiviral response and, on induction by viruses, induces autocrine cell-type-specific or autocrine non-specific signals that help mount effective innate defenses. This review covers the induction of a variety of innate immune response by the ifn system, including signal transduction, receptor binding, activation of other cytokines and expression of antiviral genes. The IFN-induced gene product, ISG, is a category of antiviral or antiproliferation genes, but the IFN-induced transcription factors may also include some genes involved in the expression of IFN- stimulated genes. This article also reviews two recently characterized types of interferon, which the authors named type I & III interferon. The type I IFN, or ‘ classical ’ or ‘ class’ IFN, was originally discovered in the serum of mice and later was shown to also exist in humans. A new class of IFNs ( type III IFN or ‘ novel ’ IFN) was identified by gene transfection and DNA microarray analyses. In addition to antiviral activity, these novel forms of IFN have been shown to have direct chemoattractant activity for monocytic leukemia cells and to modulate cellular metabolism and gene expression.
